AI.result: Circuit-level simulations show logical error rates scaling as p^t, consistent with distance-2t protection. Experimentally, using a correlated-matching decoder, increasing distance from d=4 to d=6 reduces the block logical error rate by a factor of 1.52 in both ZZ and XX memory bases.
AI.conclusion: The concatenated surface-code construction provides a compact, nearest-neighbor, single-pass-decodable fault-tolerant memory that demonstrates distance-2t scaling both in simulation and on hardware, establishing a near-term platform for concatenated architectures beyond the standard surface code.

title: When do quantum views help? Complementary classical-quantum representations in multi-view fusion
summary: Recent studies have reported promising results from quantum machine learning in drug discovery, healthcare, materials science and cybersecurity. Research includes comparisons with classical machine learning algorithms and the development of sequential hybrid pipelines. We propose that fusion can improve prediction when classical and quantum representations capture complementary predictive relationships. Our classical-quantum multi-view framework preserves the full classical input alongside simulated quantum features. Concatenation and attention combine the views; single-view comparisons, replacement and masking controls assess both views' contributions. Controlled angular-polynomial experiments distinguish targets adequately represented by a single view from those that depend on complementary angular and polynomial relationships. For these mixed targets, fusion improves prediction by combining the relevant feature sets, while matched classical representations recover the same benefit, linking the improvement to their complementary predictive content. Controlled classification tests further show that gains depend on alignment between the chosen representation and the target, and on a suitable fusion rule. Benchmark validation shows improved mean predictive performance over classical baselines on Wine, Wisconsin Diagnostic Breast Cancer, three-class Fashion-MNIST and Steel Plates Faults within the evaluated protocols. Classical replacement and masking controls remain competitive, classical baselines lead on Digits and Covertype, and outcomes with missing or corrupted views depend on the available inputs. These findings support evaluating quantum representations for their complementary predictive contribution and matching the representation and fusion strategy to the target relationships.

AI.tldr: A classical-quantum multi-view fusion framework is proposed; gains arise only when quantum and classical representations contribute complementary predictive content, evaluated via angular-polynomial targets and controlled benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Quantum machine learning has shown promise, but comparisons with classical ML and hybrid pipelines leave open whether fusion of classical and quantum views actually yields benefit. The paper argues that fusion can help only when the two representations capture complementary predictive relationships, and tests this hypothesis.
AI.method: A classical-quantum multi-view framework keeps the full classical input alongside simulated quantum features. Views are combined via concatenation and attention. Controls include single-view comparisons, classical replacement, and masking of either view. Controlled angular-polynomial experiments are designed to separate single-view-solvable targets from mixed targets requiring complementary angular and polynomial relationships. Controlled classification tests probe sensitivity to representation-target alignment and fusion rule.
AI.result: On mixed targets, fusion improves prediction by combining relevant feature sets, and matched classical representations recover the same benefit, linking gains to complementary predictive content rather than quantum-specific advantage. Classification gains depend on representation-target alignment and fusion rule. Benchmark validation shows improved mean predictive performance over classical baselines on Wine, Wisconsin Diagnostic Breast Cancer, three-class Fashion-MNIST, and Steel Plates Faults under the evaluated protocols. Classical replacement and masking controls remain competitive and classical baselines lead on Digits and Covertype; results with missing or corrupted views depend on available inputs.
AI.conclusion: Quantum representations should be evaluated by their complementary predictive contribution, not in isolation, and representation choice plus fusion strategy must be matched to the target relationships. Fusion benefits are attributable to complementary content that classical representations can also supply.

title: Parallel Repetition for Entangled Games via Conditional Relative Entropy
summary:
We give a proof of the cubic parallel-repetition bound for finite two-player entangled games using quantum conditional relative entropy. For a game with entangled value $1-\varepsilon<1$ and answer alphabets $\mathcal A,\mathcal B$, its $n$-fold repeated value is at most \[
  \exp[-Ω(\varepsilon^3n/L)],\qquad
  L:=\max\{1,\log(|\mathcal A||\mathcal B|)\}, \] for every $n\ge1$. This recovers Song's cubic rate. We also prove a threshold bound: the probability of winning a fraction at least $1-\varepsilon+δ$ is at most $\exp[-Ω(δ^5n/(\varepsilon^2L))]$ for $0<δ\le\varepsilon$.
  Our information charge is the decrease in relative entropy when a question reference is discarded. Our comparison states preserve the original conditional question law. A chain rule bounds the coordinate charges using the cost of conditioning on checked wins and retaining checked answers. Our main lemma converts small charges into nearby pure-state descriptions and local corrections, each depending only on one player's question. Together with Song's sampler, these enable approximate local preparation of the conditioned workspace.

AI.tldr: We prove the cubic parallel-repetition bound for finite two-player entangled games via quantum conditional relative entropy, recovering Song's cubic rate and additionally establishing a threshold bound.
AI.motivation: Parallel repetition bounds for entangled games are central to understanding how entangled value degrades under repetition, and prior work (Song) achieved a cubic rate. This paper aims to reprove and extend that result using an information-theoretic approach based on quantum conditional relative entropy.
AI.method: The proof uses quantum conditional relative entropy as an "information charge," defined as the decrease in relative entropy when a question reference is discarded. The comparison preserves the original conditional question law. A chain rule bounds coordinate charges via the cost of conditioning on checked wins and retaining checked answers, and a main lemma converts small charges into nearby pure-state descriptions and local corrections each depending on only one player's question. Combined with Song's sampler, these enable approximate local preparation of the conditioned workspace.
AI.result: For a game with entangled value 1-ε<1 and answer alphabets A, B, the n-fold repeated value is at most exp[-Ω(ε^3 n / L)] with L = max{1, log(|A||B|)}, for all n≥1, recovering Song's cubic rate. Additionally, the probability of winning a fraction at least 1-ε+δ is at most exp[-Ω(δ^5 n / (ε^2 L))] for 0<δ≤ε.
AI.conclusion: The quantum conditional relative entropy framework yields a self-contained proof of the cubic parallel-repetition bound and a new threshold bound, showing the information-charge method is a powerful tool for analyzing entangled game repetition.

title: Optimising multipartite entanglement manipulation in quantum networks
summary: Long-range, genuine multipartite entanglement (GME) between distant parties in a quantum network is a crucial resource for distributed quantum information processing. Through controlled manipulation of short-range GME states in the network via stochastic local operations aided by classical communication (SLOCC), long-range GME can be established between selected target nodes on demand. Optimizing such multipartite entanglement distribution protocols under constraints imposed by the network architecture, target-node set, and available resource budget is a key challenge in resource-efficient manipulation of GME. We present a general operational framework for manipulating GME in quantum networks by classifying the relevant networking operations into three broad primitives-inflation, deflation, and purification-reflecting their effect on the proliferation of GME through general bounds and illustrative examples. We show how these primitives can be combined to construct a broad class of multipartite quantum repeater protocols, enabling their systematic optimization, and demonstrate the framework with a simple example. Applying our approach to networks of Dür-Cirac-Tarrach states reveals a rich landscape of achievable end-to-end GME and accessible entanglement classes. More generally, our framework provides a systematic approach to the construction and optimization of multipartite quantum repeater protocols for scalable and resource-efficient GME distribution in quantum networks.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a general framework for distributing long-range genuine multipartite entanglement (GME) in quantum networks by classifying networking operations into three primitives—inflation, deflation, and purification—that can be composed to build and systematically optimize multipartite quantum repeater protocols.
AI.motivation: Long-range GME between distant parties is a key resource for distributed quantum information processing, and it can be established by manipulating short-range GME states via SLOCC. However, optimizing multipartite entanglement distribution under constraints from network architecture, target-node sets, and resource budgets remains a key open challenge for resource-efficient GME manipulation.
AI.method: The authors introduce an operational framework that classifies networking operations into three primitives—inflation, deflation, and purification—reflecting their effect on GME proliferation, characterized via general bounds and illustrative examples. These primitives are then composed to construct a broad class of multipartite quantum repeater protocols enabling systematic optimization, and the framework is applied to networks of Dür-Cirac-Tarrach states.
AI.result: The framework is demonstrated with a simple example and, when applied to Dür-Cirac-Tarrach state networks, reveals a rich landscape of achievable end-to-end GME and accessible entanglement classes.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework offers a systematic approach to constructing and optimizing multipartite quantum repeater protocols, supporting scalable and resource-efficient GME distribution in quantum networks.

title: Crossovers between Time-Bin and Energy-Time Entanglement in Homodyned Resonance Fluorescence
summary: We theoretically investigate photonic entanglement generated by homodyning resonance fluorescence from a two-level emitter with a phase-locked laser field. Under weak excitation, increasing the relative laser-field amplitude produces crossovers from time-bin to energy--time and back to time-bin entanglement. The intermediate energy--time regime occurs near amplitude matching, where destructive interference suppresses the single-photon component, allowing the two-photon contributions to dominate the coincidence signal. We evaluate the resulting photon statistics and first-order coherence and characterize the entanglement through violations of the CHSH Bell inequality in a Franson interferometer. This scheme provides a route to controlling photonic entanglement through linear optics and coherent interference.

AI.tldr: A two-level emitter's resonance fluorescence, homodyned with a phase-locked laser, yields tunable photonic entanglement; varying the field amplitude switches the state between time-bin and energy-time entanglement regimes.
AI.motivation: To find a controllable, linear-optics route for generating and steering photonic entanglement from a simple two-level emitter, exploiting coherent interference rather than complex nonlinear resources.
AI.method: Theoretically analyze resonance fluorescence homodyned with a phase-locked laser in the weak-excitation regime; compute photon statistics and first-order coherence, and characterize entanglement via CHSH Bell-inequality violations in a Franson interferometer as the relative laser-field amplitude is varied.
AI.result: Increasing the relative laser-field amplitude produces crossovers from time-bin to energy–time and back to time-bin entanglement. The intermediate energy–time regime emerges near amplitude matching, where destructive interference suppresses the single-photon component so two-photon contributions dominate the coincidence signal.
AI.conclusion: Homodyning resonance fluorescence with a phase-locked laser enables control of photonic entanglement via linear optics and coherent interference, offering a tunable source of time-bin and energy–time entangled photons.

title: Accurate gap control of 3D-integrated superconducting quantum circuits using asymmetric indium architecture and multi-angle flip-chip bonding
summary: Flip-chip 3D integration is a key enabling technology for overcoming the routing and layout constraints of planar superconducting quantum processors, but it requires accurate and uniform control of the inter-chip spacing while preserving qubit coherence. In conventional processes, thick indium bumps are deposited symmetrically on both chips, while dedicated spacers are introduced to limit the residual tilt. Here, we present a flip-chip bonding process based on an asymmetric indium architecture, combining $20\,μ\mathrm{m}$ thick indium bumps on the control chip with $200\,\mathrm{nm}$ thin indium pads on the qubit chip. Using electrical and microwave measurements, we demonstrate low resistance and low loss indium interconnects, and show that transmon qubits integrated with this process reach relaxation and coherence times of $T_1=(159\pm14)\,μ\mathrm{s}$ and $T_{\mathrm{2,echo}}=(294\pm42)\,μ\mathrm{s}$, respectively, comparable to planar devices. Combined with a multi angle compression procedure that suppresses systematic tilt, this approach reduces the average post bonding tilt to $(20\pm12)\,μ\mathrm{rad}$. These results establish an asymmetric indium architecture combined with multi angle compression as a robust, coherence preserving route toward 3D integrated superconducting quantum processors.

AI.tldr: An asymmetric indium flip-chip bonding process (20 μm bumps on the control chip, 200 nm pads on the qubit chip) plus a multi-angle compression procedure achieves low-loss interconnects, preserved qubit coherence (T1 = 159±14 μs, T2,echo = 294±42 μs), and reduced post-bonding tilt of (20±12) μrad.
AI.motivation: Flip-chip 3D integration is needed to overcome routing and layout constraints of planar superconducting quantum processors, but conventional processes require thick symmetric indium bumps on both chips and dedicated spacers to control inter-chip spacing and residual tilt. There is a need for a simpler, robust process that ensures accurate and uniform inter-chip spacing while preserving qubit coherence.
AI.method: The authors develop a flip-chip bonding process based on an asymmetric indium architecture: 20 μm thick indium bumps on the control chip and 200 nm thin indium pads on the qubit chip, eliminating the need for symmetric thick bumps and dedicated spacers. They characterize the interconnects via electrical (resistance) and microwave (loss) measurements, integrate transmon qubits with the process to measure coherence, and apply a multi-angle compression procedure to suppress systematic tilt, quantifying the resulting post-bonding tilt.
AI.result: The indium interconnects exhibit low resistance and low microwave loss. Transmon qubits integrated with the process show T1 = (159±14) μs and T2,echo = (294±42) μs, comparable to planar devices. The multi-angle compression procedure reduces the average post-bonding tilt to (20±12) μrad.
AI.conclusion: The asymmetric indium architecture combined with multi-angle compression provides a robust, coherence-preserving route toward 3D-integrated superconducting quantum processors, offering accurate spacing and tilt control without symmetric thick bumps or dedicated spacers.

title: Casimir forces on suspended thin dielectric membranes covered with graphene
summary: We investigate the Casimir force on thin suspended dielectric layers covered with graphene, both theoretically and experimentally. Thermal effects of the Casimir force on graphene occur at separations significantly smaller compared to ordinary metals and dielectrics. At such small separations, the Casimir force is sufficiently strong to be measured experimentally. However, the presence of substrates to support the graphene significantly reduces the enhancement. We show theoretically that replacing the solid substrate beneath graphene with a thin dielectric membrane partially restores this strong thermal dependence. One of the interacting objects is a solid gold plate. The other object is a suspended dielectric membrane made of either 15 nm of silicon oxide or 13 nm silicon nitride, covered with graphene. At a separation of $\sim$500 nm, theoretical predictions yield changes in the Casimir pressure of up to 54 % and 40 % for silicon oxide and silicon nitride, respectively, when the temperature is increased from 10 K to 294 K. Measurements were performed for graphene on a suspended silicon nitride membrane at room temperature, using a gold-coated sphere attached to a cantilever as the force sensor. The measured force gradient is consistent with the theoretical prediction, although the thermal dependence could not be resolved, in part because of uncertainties in the optical properties of silicon nitride. Replacing a bulk substrate with a thin dielectric membrane covered with graphene provides a substantial reduction of the Casimir force, which may facilitate the stable operation of neutral nanomechanical elements at small separations.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how replacing a bulk substrate with a thin dielectric membrane beneath graphene enhances the thermal dependence of the Casimir force, theoretically predicting large temperature-driven pressure changes at ~500 nm separation, and experimentally testing graphene on a suspended SiN membrane at room temperature.
AI.motivation: Graphene shows strong thermal Casimir effects at separations much smaller than ordinary metals and dielectrics, where the force is strong enough to measure, but a supporting solid substrate suppresses this enhancement. The authors aim to recover the strong thermal dependence by using a thin suspended dielectric membrane instead of a bulk substrate.
AI.method: Theoretical calculations of the Casimir force/pressure between a gold plate and a suspended dielectric membrane (15 nm SiO2 or 13 nm SiN) covered with graphene, evaluated for temperature changes from 10 K to 294 K at ~500 nm separation. Experiment: force-gradient measurements using a gold-coated sphere on a cantilever as the force sensor interacting with graphene on a suspended SiN membrane at room temperature.
AI.result: Theory predicts up to 54% (SiO2) and 40% (SiN) change in Casimir pressure from 10 K to 294 K at ~500 nm. The measured force gradient for graphene on suspended SiN at room temperature agrees with theory, although the thermal dependence could not be resolved, partly due to uncertainty in the optical properties of SiN.
AI.conclusion: Replacing a bulk substrate with a thin graphene-covered dielectric membrane partially restores the strong thermal dependence of the Casimir force and substantially reduces the force, which may enable stable operation of neutral nanomechanical elements at small separations.

title: Periodic conditional measurements on a photonic chip
summary: Quantum measurements not only extract information but also reshape quantum evolution through measurement backaction. Here, we investigate periodic conditional measurements, in which coherent evolution is repeatedly interrupted by local measurements. We show that the bright and dark modes of the conditional evolution operator provide a unified spectral description of both the post-selected final state along no-detection trajectories and the statistics of detection events. Using a three-dimensional photonic chip, we demonstrate on-demand state engineering through dark-mode preservation and bright-mode selection, enabling the protection of topological corner states and excited-state shelving. We further observe the predicted transition of the total detection probability on an effectively infinite one-dimensional lattice and identify its microscopic origin in Floquet near-dark modes. These results establish periodic conditional measurements as a general framework for engineering conditional quantum states and manipulating event-detection statistics in monitored quantum dynamics.

AI.tldr: Periodic conditional measurements reshape quantum dynamics; bright/dark modes of the conditional evolution operator give a unified spectral description of no-detection post-selected states and detection statistics, demonstrated on a 3D photonic chip for state engineering and topological protection.
AI.motivation: Quantum measurements not only extract information but also reshape quantum evolution via measurement backaction. The authors seek a unified framework to understand and exploit periodically interrupted coherent evolution for both conditional-state engineering and controlling event-detection statistics.
AI.method: They study periodic conditional measurements where coherent evolution is repeatedly interrupted by local measurements. They show that bright and dark modes of the conditional evolution operator provide a unified spectral description of (i) the post-selected final state along no-detection trajectories and (ii) detection-event statistics. Experiments are performed on a three-dimensional photonic chip.
AI.result: On-demand state engineering is demonstrated via dark-mode preservation and bright-mode selection, enabling protection of topological corner states and excited-state shelving. They also observe the predicted transition of total detection probability on an effectively infinite 1D lattice and identify its microscopic origin in Floquet near-dark modes.
AI.conclusion: Periodic conditional measurements constitute a general framework for engineering conditional quantum states and manipulating event-detection statistics in monitored quantum dynamics.

title: Limits of adaptive linear postprocessing in six-state quantum key distribution
summary: Two-way classical communication improves the noise tolerance of quantum key distribution, but the limits of adaptive parity processing remain unclear. For the six-state protocol with equal three-basis error rate $p\in[p_*,1/2]$, where $p_*=(5-\sqrt5)/10\simeq27.64\%$, we construct a single compatible collective attack that defeats a broad class of linear postprocessing. Each public message may be an affine function of the sender's raw key, chosen adaptively from the public history. For every finite input length and every accepted transcript of positive probability, Eve's optimal probability of recovering any affine function of Alice's raw key is at least Bob's. Consequently, reliable agreement on a linear final key is incompatible with secrecy. The same conclusion holds for arbitrary publicly seeded privacy amplification after reliable recovery of a linear candidate. The proof conditions on the complete transcript, which restricts the two raw keys to affine subspaces. A local degradation of Eve's state, a known Rényi-entropy comparison, and a coset-probability inequality then give the recovery comparison. Both inequalities are proved in self-contained appendices. The result allows block splitting, regrouping, nonzero-syndrome selection, and adaptive linear reconciliation.

AI.tldr: For the six-state QKD protocol at error rate p ≥ (5−√5)/10, a single compatible collective attack defeats all linear/affine adaptive two-way postprocessing, showing reliable linear-key agreement is incompatible with secrecy.
AI.motivation: Two-way classical communication raises the noise tolerance of QKD, but the ultimate limits of adaptive parity (linear) processing were unclear. The paper aims to establish a sharp impossibility boundary for such postprocessing in the six-state protocol.
AI.method: Constructs one collective attack compatible with the protocol for equal three-basis error rate p∈[p*,1/2], p*=(5−√5)/10≈27.64%. Each public message may be any affine function of the sender's raw key chosen adaptively from the public history. The proof conditions on the full transcript (restricting both raw keys to affine subspaces) and combines a local degradation of Eve's state, a known Rényi-entropy comparison, and a coset-probability inequality (both proved in self-contained appendices).
AI.result: For every finite input length and every accepted positive-probability transcript, Eve's optimal probability of recovering any affine function of Alice's raw key is at least Bob's. Hence reliable agreement on a linear final key is incompatible with secrecy, even with arbitrary publicly seeded privacy amplification following reliable recovery of a linear candidate. The attack covers block splitting, regrouping, nonzero-syndrome selection, and adaptive linear reconciliation.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive linear/affine two-way reconciliation cannot push the six-state protocol beyond p*≈27.64%; beyond this threshold no linear-key protocol can be both correct and secret against the constructed collective attack, delimiting the power of parity-based postprocessing.

title: Finite-Frequency Boson-Number Bounds Across the Quantum Rabi Transition
summary: We consider the quantum Rabi model, a fundamental model of quantum optics describing a two-level system coupled to a bosonic mode, including counter-rotating terms. In the limit of large separation between the two-level transition frequency and the bosonic mode frequency, the model exhibits a quantum phase transition at a critical coupling strength. Although the model is exactly solvable, simple analytic expressions for important physical quantities are generally unavailable. We derive rigorous upper and lower bounds for the ground-state energy and boson occupation number across the quantum phase transition at finite frequency ratios. Our results characterize the subcritical, critical, and supercritical regimes and establish the scaling behavior of the boson occupation near the critical point. Exact numerical diagonalization demonstrates the tightness of the derived bounds, while the resulting finite-frequency inequalities provide experimentally testable predictions for trapped-ion quantum simulators.

AI.tldr: Rigorous upper and lower bounds are derived for the ground-state energy and boson occupation number of the quantum Rabi model across its quantum phase transition at finite frequency ratios, capturing subcritical, critical, and supercritical regimes and the critical scaling of boson occupation.
AI.motivation: The quantum Rabi model, despite being exactly solvable, lacks simple analytic expressions for key physical quantities, particularly across its quantum phase transition in the large-detuning limit.
AI.method: Analytical derivation of rigorous upper and lower bounds for the ground-state energy and boson occupation number across the transition at finite frequency ratios, validated against exact numerical diagonalization.
AI.result: The bounds characterize the subcritical, critical, and supercritical regimes, establish the scaling behavior of boson occupation near the critical point, and are shown numerically to be tight; the finite-frequency inequalities yield experimentally testable predictions for trapped-ion quantum simulators.
AI.conclusion: The derived finite-frequency bounds provide a rigorous, quantitatively tight analytic characterization of the quantum Rabi model's phase transition with direct relevance to trapped-ion quantum simulation experiments.

title: Reducing the Cost of Qudit State Preparation by Learning a Sparse Structure for SNAP Gates
comment: 16 pages, 3 figures, 4 tables, accepted at International Workshop on AI for Quantum and Quantum for AI (AIQxQIA 2026), co-located with AIxIA 2026, Perugia, Italy
summary: Preparing quantum states in bosonic qudits with SNAP--Displacement sequences requires both optimizing the gate parameters and deciding which Fock levels should be controlled by each SNAP gate. A fully parameterized ansatz assigns an independent phase to every Fock level in every gate, leading to a number of phases that grows steeply. This constitutes a problem for short to medium term systems as controlling many phases requires complex control pulses which are subject to increased control errors. Previous work reduced this cost by restricting the trainable phases to predefined sparse patterns, such as a diagonal or a grid, which however may not be optimal for a specific target state. In this work, we address this limitation by introducing a method that learns which phases are needed together with their values, using a differentiable mask. A sparsity penalty encourages the removal of unnecessary phases, while temperature annealing gradually turns the masks into binary decisions. We compare the proposed method with fully parameterized and predefined sparse ansatzes on Fourier and Haar-random target states. The evaluation considers both the minimum number of phases required to reach different infidelity thresholds and the overall trade-off between fidelity and phases required, measured through Pareto frontiers and hypervolume. The results show that learning the location of the phases together with their values provides competitive or improved fidelity--resource trade-offs, although the advantage depends on the target state and qudit dimension.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a differentiable-mask method that jointly learns which Fock-level phases to keep in SNAP–Displacement sequences and their values, using a sparsity penalty and temperature annealing to binarize the masks, and benchmarks it against fully parameterized and predefined sparse ansatzes.
AI.motivation: Fully parameterized ansatzes assign an independent phase to every Fock level in every SNAP gate, so the number of phases grows steeply; controlling many phases requires complex pulses that incur increased control errors, which is problematic for short- to medium-term systems. Prior sparse approaches restrict trainable phases to predefined patterns (diagonal, grid) that may be suboptimal for a given target state.
AI.method: A differentiable mask is used to learn phase locations jointly with their values; a sparsity penalty removes unnecessary phases, and temperature annealing gradually converts the masks into binary decisions.
AI.result: Compared on Fourier and Haar-random target states, evaluating both the minimum number of phases needed to reach different infidelity thresholds and the fidelity–resource trade-off via Pareto frontiers and hypervolume, the learned-location approach yields competitive or improved trade-offs, with the advantage depending on the target state and qudit dimension.
AI.conclusion: Learning both the location and value of phases is a viable way to reduce control resources in SNAP–Displacement state preparation, though its benefit is not universal and depends on the target state and qudit dimension.

title: Time-optimal robust quantum control for partially known errors
comment: 11 pages total, 7 pages main text, 2 figures
summary: Robust quantum control usually assumes one of two extremes: the error is of a known form and only its strength is unknown, or nothing at all is known about it. In practice one often sits in between. The size of a static error is unknown, but its class is known, for example, it only shifts energy levels, or it acts on each subsystem separately. We ask how fast a control can cancel, to first order, every error in such a class. A time-independent Hamiltonian can do this if and only if all errors in the class have zero diagonal in a common basis. In that case an equally spaced energy ladder in this basis does it after one period. A lower bound that holds for any time-dependent control with bounded drive power shows that this simple constant control is optimal for several natural classes, including unknown level shifts and unknown local errors on two subsystems. Completely unknown errors need a time-dependent control, and there, knowing the error class shortens the minimum time by a factor $\sqrt{d^2+1}$. So partial knowledge of the error changes not only how long an optimal robust control takes, but also its form.

AI.tldr: The paper studies robust quantum control under partial knowledge of errors: the error's class is known but its magnitude is not. It shows a time-independent Hamiltonian cancels all errors in a class to first order iff they have vanishing diagonal in a common basis, and that a constant equally spaced energy ladder achieves this optimally, with time-dependent controls needed only for completely unknown errors.
AI.motivation: Robust control typically assumes errors are either of fully known form with unknown strength, or entirely unknown. Realistic settings lie in between: the size of a static error is unknown but its class is known (e.g., it only shifts energy levels or acts on each subsystem separately). The authors ask how fast a control can cancel, to first order, every error in such a class.
AI.method: The analysis characterizes first-order cancellation of a family of static errors using a time-independent Hamiltonian, deriving a necessary and sufficient condition (zero diagonal of all errors in a common basis) and constructing an equally spaced energy ladder in that basis that cancels the errors after one period. A lower bound applicable to any time-dependent control with bounded drive power is derived and compared against this simple constant control for several natural error classes.
AI.result: A time-independent Hamiltonian can cancel the class to first order iff all errors have zero diagonal in a common basis; an equally spaced ladder then works after one period. The lower bound proves this constant control is optimal for several natural classes, including unknown level shifts and unknown local errors on two subsystems. For completely unknown errors a time-dependent control is required, and knowing the error class reduces the minimum time by a factor of sqrt(d^2+1).
AI.conclusion: Partial knowledge of the error class changes both the minimum achievable time and the form of the optimal robust control: static constant controls can be optimal for structured error classes, while genuinely unknown errors demand time-dependent driving. This positions the degree of prior error knowledge as a central design parameter in robust quantum control.

title: Practical Fidelity Estimation for Noisy Quantum Devices Using Direct and Survival-Probability-Based Protocols
summary: Reliable characterization of quantum states and quantum processes is central to the development of scalable quantum computing. Standard characterization techniques such as full quantum state tomography become rapidly impractical as system size increases. In this work we present two software-oriented fidelity estimation protocols that avoid full tomographic reconstruction while remaining experimentally relevant for noisy intermediate-scale quantum devices. The first protocol is direct fidelity estimation (DFE), where the fidelity between a target state and an experimentally prepared state is estimated from importance-sampled Pauli measurements. The second protocol is a survival-probability-based method that reconstructs fidelity from experimentally accessible moments of a noisy evolution and its approximate inverse, and is intrinsically robust against state-preparation-and-measurement (SPAM) errors. We discuss the theoretical basis of both approaches, analyze their noise sensitivity, and present numerical evidence on representative multiqubit states under depolarizing, dephasing, and amplitude-damping channels. For DFE we show that attenuation-aware correction improves robustness against measurement noise. For the survival-probability approach we show that an $L_2$-optimized expansion substantially outperforms naive Taylor truncation in high-noise regimes.

AI.tldr: Two software-oriented fidelity estimation protocols—direct fidelity estimation (DFE) and a survival-probability-based method—are presented to characterize quantum states and processes without full tomography, with noise-robust refinements validated numerically.
AI.motivation: Full quantum state tomography becomes impractical as system size grows, yet reliable characterization of states and processes is essential for scalable quantum computing. The work aims for protocols that avoid full tomographic reconstruction while remaining experimentally relevant for noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) devices.
AI.method: Protocol 1: DFE, estimating fidelity between a target and prepared state via importance-sampled Pauli measurements, augmented with attenuation-aware correction. Protocol 2: a survival-probability method reconstructing fidelity from experimentally accessible moments of a noisy evolution and its approximate inverse, giving intrinsic robustness to SPAM errors; an L2-optimized expansion replaces naive Taylor truncation.
AI.result: Theoretical bases and noise-sensitivity analyses are provided, with numerical evidence on representative multiqubit states under depolarizing, dephasing, and amplitude-damping channels. Attenuation-aware correction improves DFE robustness against measurement noise, and the L2-optimized expansion substantially outperforms naive Taylor truncation in high-noise regimes.
AI.conclusion: Both protocols offer practical, scalable fidelity estimation alternatives to full tomography for NISQ devices, with tailored corrections and expansions that markedly improve performance under noise.

title: Driving the cooling process of a quantum system via classical noise
summary: It is known that under particular hypotheses anomalous thermalization processes can occur, such as the Mpemba effect, consisting in a faster cooling down when the system is prepared in a hotter initial condition, thus making convenient to warm up the system before the freezing process in order to make it freeze in a shorter time. It is shown here that the action of a Markovian classical noise during the freezing process can accelerate the approach to the zero-temperature thermal state. This prediction is counterintuitive, especially after observing that a classical noise can be considered equivalent to the action of an infinite-temperature reservoir, since both drive the system toward the same state. These facts lead to the statement that warming up the system during the contact with a low-temperature reservoir can accelerate the cooling process.

AI.tldr: A Markovian classical noise applied during freezing can accelerate convergence to the zero-temperature thermal state—counterintuitive since noise mimics an infinite-temperature reservoir—implying that warming a system while in contact with a cold bath can speed up cooling.
AI.motivation: Anomalous thermalization phenomena such as the Mpemba effect show that a hotter initial condition can cool faster, motivating an investigation of whether adding thermal noise (equivalently, an infinite-temperature reservoir) during the freezing process itself can accelerate approach to the T=0 thermal state.
AI.method: Theoretical analysis using a classical Markovian noise model acting on the system during the freezing (cooling) dynamics, treating the noise as equivalent to an infinite-temperature reservoir that drives the system toward the same target state.
AI.result: The action of Markovian classical noise during freezing is shown to accelerate the approach to the zero-temperature thermal state, even though the noise drives the system toward the same state as the cold bath.
AI.conclusion: Warming a system during contact with a low-temperature reservoir can accelerate the cooling process, extending anomalous thermalization behavior (Mpemba-like) to the presence of noise and yielding a counterintuitive but rigorous prediction.

title: Quantum instanton approach to metastable collective spin systems: Numerical implementation and applications
comment: 23 pages, 11 figures. Companion paper to arXiv:2604.15091
summary: Driven-dissipative collective spin systems can host several long-lived metastable states; rare switching between them governs slow relaxation and first-order dissipative phase transitions associated with changes in the dominant stationary state. In the companion Letter [arXiv:2604.15091], we introduced a quantum instanton framework based on exact quasiprobability dynamics to describe this switching and illustrated it with a minimal model possessing a simplifying symmetry. Here we develop its numerical implementation, combining collocation and shooting methods, and apply it to two microscopically motivated systems: the Lipkin-Meshkov-Glick model with purely collective dissipation and the cooperative resonance fluorescence with collective and local dissipation. By determining the leading exponential scaling of switching rates between metastable attractors, we predict the stationary magnetization, the first-order dissipative phase-transition point, and the exponential scaling of slow relaxation rates. These predictions agree with quantum master-equation calculations and an exact analytical result for the second model without dephasing. We also examine how the choice of quasiprobability representation affects numerical convergence and find that the alternative semiclassical Wigner approach, based on Gaussian truncation, has varying accuracy across models and parameter regimes. These results substantiate the framework's applicability to experimentally relevant collective spin systems with both collective and local dissipation.

AI.tldr: This paper develops the numerical implementation of a quantum instanton framework for metastable switching in driven-dissipative collective spin systems, using collocation and shooting methods, and validates it on the Lipkin-Meshkov-Glick model and cooperative resonance fluorescence.
AI.motivation: Rare switching between long-lived metastable states governs slow relaxation and first-order dissipative phase transitions in driven-dissipative collective spin systems. The companion Letter introduced a quasiprobability-based quantum instanton framework on a symmetric minimal model; here the authors need a practical numerical scheme applicable to microscopically motivated, experimentally relevant systems with both collective and local dissipation.
AI.method: The authors build the numerics for exact quasiprobability instanton dynamics by combining collocation and shooting methods to extract the leading exponential scaling of switching rates between metastable attractors. They apply this to the Lipkin-Meshkov-Glick model with purely collective dissipation and to cooperative resonance fluorescence with collective and local dissipation, and compare representation choices (exact quasiprobability vs. semiclassical Wigner/Gaussian truncation) for convergence.
AI.result: From the leading exponential scaling of switching rates, they predict stationary magnetization, the first-order dissipative phase-transition point, and exponential scaling of slow relaxation rates. These predictions agree with quantum master-equation calculations and, for the second model without dephasing, with an exact analytical result. The Wigner/Gaussian-truncation approach shows varying accuracy across models and parameter regimes.
AI.conclusion: The instanton framework is numerically workable and applicable to experimentally relevant collective spin systems with combined collective and local dissipation; quasiprobability representation choice materially affects numerical convergence, with the exact quasiprobability approach being the reliable workhorse and Wigner semiclassics only conditionally accurate.

title: Size-Dependent High-Order Harmonic Generation from Linear Carbon-Chain Molecules in Linearly Polarized Laser Fields
summary: High-order harmonic generation from molecules is highly sensitive to molecular geometry and strong-field electron dynamics, providing a powerful route for probing and controlling ultrafast processes in extended systems. In this work, we systematically investigate the influence of molecular chain length on HHG from linear carbon-chain molecules C$_2$H$_2$, C$_6$H$_2$, and C$_{10}$H$_2$ driven by an 800 nm linearly polarized laser field. To isolate the molecular-size effect from the influence of different ionization potentials, the laser intensities are adjusted to maintain the same Keldysh parameter for different molecules. Real-time time-dependent density functional theory simulations are performed with the molecular axis aligned parallel to the laser polarization direction. The results show that increasing the molecular chain length significantly enhances the harmonic yield and tends to extend the cutoff region. In particular, C$_{10}$H$_2$ exhibits much stronger plateau harmonics than C$_2$H$_2$, while the intermediate molecule C$_6$H$_2$ shows harmonic intensities between those of C$_2$H$_2$ and C$_{10}$H$_2$. Time-frequency analysis and charge-density evolution reveal that the enhanced HHG emission in longer chains originates from the enlarged electron acceleration distance and increased probability of multi-center recollision, especially near the terminal carbon atoms. These findings demonstrate that molecular-size engineering offers an effective strategy for controlling harmonic emission and optimizing attosecond light sources in extended molecular systems.

AI.tldr: Increasing carbon-chain length (C2H2→C6H2→C10H2) at matched Keldysh parameter enhances HHG yield and extends the cutoff, driven by longer electron acceleration paths and multi-center recollision near terminal carbons.
AI.motivation: HHG in molecules is sensitive to geometry and strong-field electron dynamics, making it a probe of ultrafast processes in extended systems. The study aims to isolate the pure molecular-size effect on HHG from the confounding influence of differing ionization potentials, thereby clarifying how chain length governs harmonic emission.
AI.method: Real-time time-dependent density functional theory (RT-TDDFT) simulations of linear carbon chains C2H2, C6H2, and C10H2 driven by an 800 nm linearly polarized field, with molecular axis parallel to polarization. Laser intensities were tuned per molecule to hold the Keldysh parameter constant, decoupling size from ionization potential. Time-frequency analysis and charge-density evolution were used to identify emission mechanisms.
AI.result: Longer chains markedly increase harmonic yield and tend to extend the cutoff. C10H2 shows far stronger plateau harmonics than C2H2, with C6H2 intermediate. Analysis attributes the enhancement to larger electron acceleration distances and higher multi-center recollision probability, particularly near terminal carbon atoms.
AI.conclusion: Molecular-size engineering via chain-length control is an effective strategy for tuning harmonic emission and optimizing attosecond light sources in extended molecular systems.

title: Operator-Space Entanglement Entropy in Random Fermionic Gaussian Dynamics
summary: We study the von Neumann operator-space entanglement entropy (OSEE) of initial product operators evolved under random gaussian dynamics, as modeled by a Brownian SYK$_2$ model. By exploiting a mapping to a domain-wall melting problem, we derive an exact expression for the time-dependent bipartite OSEE in the thermodynamic limit, and obtain an analytic characterization of the corresponding gaussian Page curve emerging at late times. Our results build on recent work on the entanglement dynamics in the all-to-all quantum simple exclusion process, leveraging tools from RMT, including the Coulomb-gas approach and a mapping to the free Jacobi process. Finally, based on our results, we discuss the possibility of relating the OSEE with non-gaussianity measures in the Heisenberg picture.

AI.tldr: Exact time-dependent von Neumann operator-space entanglement entropy for product operators under Brownian SYK$_2$ dynamics, via a domain-wall melting mapping, with an analytic late-time gaussian Page curve.
AI.motivation: Operator-space entanglement entropy (OSEE) of operators evolving under random gaussian dynamics is poorly characterized analytically; the authors aim for an exact, thermodynamic-limit description and to connect it to non-gaussianity measures in the Heisenberg picture.
AI.method: Study of a Brownian SYK$_2$ model; mapping to a domain-wall melting problem; leverage of random matrix theory tools (Coulomb-gas approach, mapping to the free Jacobi process), building on results for the all-to-all quantum simple exclusion process.
AI.result: Exact expression for the time-dependent bipartite OSEE in the thermodynamic limit, plus an analytic characterization of the gaussian Page curve at late times.
AI.conclusion: The OSEE dynamics admits an exact solvable description whose late-time behavior follows a gaussian Page curve, and the results suggest a possible link between OSEE and non-gaussianity measures in the Heisenberg picture.

title: Remote Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill Entanglement Generation between Trapped Ions
summary: Distributing entanglement directly between error-corrected logical qubits is an important capability for scalable quantum networks. We propose a heralded protocol for generating remote entanglement between Gottesman--Kitaev--Preskill qubits encoded in the motional modes of spatially separated trapped ions, using the internal electronic states to interface the motional qubits with emitted photons. We derive the protocol for single-rail and polarization photonic encodings and evaluate the effects of finite GKP squeezing, photon loss, photon recoil, motional heating, and motional dephasing on the decoded logical state. Moreover, we numerically analysed the fidelity of distributed logical Bell-pair fidelity. We find that one can achieve more than 95% of fidelity in the realistic situation. The protocol combines motional-control and photonic-networking operations that have already been demonstrated in trapped-ion experiments.

AI.tldr: Proposes a heralded protocol to entangle GKP logical qubits encoded in motional modes of distant trapped ions via photons, showing >95% distributed Bell-pair fidelity under realistic noise.
AI.motivation: Scalable quantum networks require distributing entanglement directly between error-corrected logical qubits rather than physical qubits, motivating a logical-level remote entanglement scheme compatible with trapped-ion hardware.
AI.method: Encodes GKP qubits in motional modes of spatially separated trapped ions, using internal electronic states to interface motional qubits with emitted photons. Derives the protocol for single-rail and polarization photonic encodings, and evaluates effects of finite GKP squeezing, photon loss, photon recoil, motional heating, and motional dephasing on the decoded logical state, with numerical analysis of distributed logical Bell-pair fidelity.
AI.result: More than 95% fidelity for distributed logical Bell pairs in the realistic regime; fidelity characterized as a function of finite GKP squeezing and dominant noise channels.
AI.conclusion: Logical entanglement between remote trapped-ion GKP qubits is achievable using only already-demonstrated motional-control and photonic-networking primitives, providing a practical route toward error-corrected quantum networks.

title: Local finite rate semi device independent randomness expansion from quantum contextuality
summary: Finite rate randomness expansion (RE) which is secure against quantum adversaries is a crucial information processing task which is well studied in the case of two non-communicating parties sharing Bell non-local correlations in a device independent manner. In this paper we show that contextual correlations with only a single localized party are sufficient for RE in a semi-device independent (SDI) manner. We propose a template SDI-RE protocol which is applicable for arbitrary $N$-cycle non-contextuality (NC) inequalities and derive its RE rate under finite statistics. As a special case, we also highlight the advantages of the situation when RE is constrained by Clauser-Horne-Shimony-Holt (CHSH) inequality but with characterized measurements implemented by only a single party. Our template protocol also incorporates non-ideal statistics which may not satisfy perfect commutativity and perfect repeatability, both of which are necessary in a loophole-free test of NC inequalities. As such, several recent experimental implementations of significantly loophole-free tests of NC inequalities can be modified for secure RE following our approach.

AI.tldr: The paper establishes that contextual correlations involving only a single localized party suffice for finite-rate randomness expansion (RE) in a semi-device-independent (SDI) manner, providing a template protocol applicable to arbitrary N-cycle non-contextuality inequalities, including a CHSH-based special case.
AI.motivation: Standard device-independent RE relies on two non-communicating parties sharing Bell non-local correlations, which imposes strong experimental demands. The authors seek a less demanding route to secure randomness expansion against quantum adversaries, exploiting contextuality with a single localized party instead of full Bell non-locality.
AI.method: The authors propose a template SDI-RE protocol valid for arbitrary N-cycle non-contextuality (NC) inequalities and derive its finite-statistics randomness expansion rate. They analyze the special case of RE constrained by the CHSH inequality with characterized measurements performed by only one party, and the protocol is designed to accommodate non-ideal statistics lacking perfect commutativity and perfect repeatability.
AI.result: The template protocol yields a finite-rate randomness expansion guarantee from single-party contextuality across arbitrary N-cycle NC inequalities, and the CHSH-based single-party-characterized-measurement case is shown to offer distinctive advantages. The protocol remains valid under non-ideal statistics, so existing loophole-free (or near loophole-free) NC inequality experiments can be repurposed for secure RE.
AI.conclusion: Contextual correlations with a single localized party are sufficient for semi-device-independent randomness expansion, relaxing the two-party requirement of Bell-based DI-RE. The framework tolerates realistic experimental imperfections and thereby connects recent loophole-free contextuality tests to practical secure randomness generation.

title: Same Spectrum, Harder First-Order Training: Phase-Locking in Single- versus Multi-Qubit Re-Uploading Circuits
summary: Angle-encoded variational quantum circuits implement truncated Fourier series. For one-dimensional inputs, a single-qubit re-uploading (serial) circuit represents every function that a multi-qubit circuit with the same encoding budget $E$ can; we find that this exchange of width for depth is not free in first-order training. Because its state lives on the Bloch sphere, all parameters of the serial circuit move the state, at each input, along one complex direction, which we call \emph{phase-locking}. We prove that this costs no Fourier direction but leaves no direction to spare: however many parameters it has, the serial circuit has at most $2E+2$ tangent directions, one more than its $2E+1$ Fourier coefficients need, while a two-qubit control with the same encoding budget and model class generically has at least $6E+6$. The cost in training is measured against this control, as the number of runs out of 100 that reach the optimum within a fixed step budget. On an exact loss with flat-spectrum targets the gap grows with $E$; at $E=32$ the serial circuit converges in 3, 53 and 83 runs under gradient descent, Adam and Levenberg--Marquardt, the control in 99, 100 and 100. On three real-world series, at matched parameter counts, the serial circuit reaches the least-squares optimum in at most 9 runs under Adam and in 32 to 93 under Levenberg--Marquardt, the control in at least 98 and in all 100; its held-out error is up to about $1.5$ times that of the control under Adam, but no larger in the typical run under Levenberg--Marquardt.

AI.tldr: Single-qubit re-uploading (serial) quantum circuits can represent the same functions as wider multi-qubit circuits at equal encoding budget E, but prove harder to train: phase-locking caps their tangent-space dimension at 2E+2 versus at least 6E+6 for a two-qubit control, producing large convergence-rate gaps that widen with E.
AI.motivation: Angle-encoded variational circuits realize truncated Fourier series, and prior work shows a one-dimensional single-qubit re-uploading circuit matches the expressivity of a multi-qubit circuit with the same encoding budget E. The open question is whether trading width for depth is free under first-order training, i.e., whether expressivity parity translates into comparable trainability and optimization behavior.
AI.method: The authors characterize the local geometry of serial re-uploading circuits: since the state lies on the Bloch sphere, all parameters move the state, at each input, along a single complex direction (phase-locking). They derive bounds on the tangent-space (Jacobi) dimension of the serial circuit (at most 2E+2) and compare with a two-qubit control with the same encoding budget and model class (generically at least 6E+6). Empirically they measure training success as runs out of 100 reaching the optimum within a fixed step budget, using gradient descent, Adam, and Levenberg-Marquardt, on an exact loss with flat-spectrum targets and on three real-world time series at matched parameter counts, also reporting held-out error.
AI.result: On the exact loss with flat-spectrum targets, the trainability gap grows with E: at E=32 the serial circuit converges in 3, 53, and 83 of 100 runs under gradient descent, Adam, and Levenberg-Marquardt respectively, versus 99, 100, and 100 for the control. On three real-world series at matched parameter counts, the serial circuit reaches the least-squares optimum in at most 9 runs under Adam and 32-93 under Levenberg-Marquardt, while the control reaches it in at least 98 and in all 100 runs. Held-out error of the serial circuit is up to ~1.5x that of the control under Adam but no larger in the typical run under Levenberg-Marquardt.
AI.conclusion: Exchanging width for depth in angle-encoded circuits preserves Fourier expressivity but not trainability: phase-locking restricts the serial circuit's tangent space to 2E+2 directions, just one above its Fourier coefficient count, leaving no spare optimization directions and yielding markedly worse first-order convergence that worsens with encoding budget. Second-order methods (Levenberg-Marquardt) largely recover the gap, and held-out accuracy can be comparable in typical runs despite slower optimization.

title: Quantum-compatible Riemannian conjugate gradient for ground-state preparation
summary: Riemannian optimization provides a natural geometric framework for designing quantum algorithms for ground-state preparation, most notably through quantum imaginary-time evolution. However, existing geometry-aware approaches primarily employ steepest-descent updates, leaving more advanced methods from classical Riemannian optimization largely unexplored. In this work, we introduce quantum conjugate gradient descent (QCGD), a quantum-compatible implementation of Riemannian conjugate gradient that combines the steepest descent direction with information retained from previous search directions. In our numerical experiments, the proposed approach achieves faster convergence per iteration than the baseline double-bracket quantum imaginary-time evolution (DB-QITE) algorithm, and we quantify the associated circuit cost with gate counts produced by Qrisp. This improvement, however, comes at the cost of increased circuit depth for each update step, revealing a trade-off between convergence rate and implementation complexity. Nevertheless, since the circuit depth for those algorithms grows exponentially with the number of iterations, the proposed method may offer practical advantages, particularly in the early fault-tolerant regime.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces quantum conjugate gradient descent (QCGD), a quantum-compatible Riemannian conjugate gradient method for ground-state preparation that reuses previous search directions to accelerate convergence relative to double-bracket quantum imaginary-time evolution (DB-QITE), at the cost of deeper circuits per step.
AI.motivation: Riemannian optimization offers a natural geometric framework for quantum ground-state preparation, exemplified by quantum imaginary-time evolution. Yet existing geometry-aware quantum algorithms rely almost exclusively on steepest-descent updates, so more advanced classical Riemannian optimization techniques remain unexplored.
AI.method: The authors formulate QCGD as a quantum-compatible implementation of Riemannian conjugate gradient, combining the steepest-descent direction with information retained from prior search directions. Numerical experiments benchmark it against DB-QITE, and circuit cost is quantified via gate counts generated with Qrisp.
AI.result: QCGD achieves faster convergence per iteration than the DB-QITE baseline in numerical experiments, but each update step requires increased circuit depth, exposing a trade-off between convergence rate and implementation complexity.
AI.conclusion: Because circuit depth of such algorithms grows exponentially with the number of iterations, faster per-iteration convergence may make QCGD practically advantageous, particularly in the early fault-tolerant regime.

title: Controlled-Memory Identification with Shared Generators: Dimension--Horizon Tradeoffs and Quantum--Classical Separation
summary: We determine the finite-horizon identification limits of a \(d\)-dimensional memory when the control interface is restricted to four shared, time-homogeneous generators. A writer encodes a message by applying a prefix word to a common root state. The verifier then applies a candidate-dependent query word followed by a shared terminal binary test, with each word of length at most \(T\). For fixed error tolerances \(λ_2>0\) and \(λ_1+λ_2<1\), the optimal identification sizes satisfy \(\ln N_{\mathsf Q,4}=Θ_{λ_1,λ_2}(\min\{d^2,T\})\) for arbitrary CPTP generators and \(\ln N_{\mathsf S,4}=Θ_{λ_1,λ_2}(\min\{d,T\})\) for stochastic maps. Four unitary letters and four permutation letters attain these respective bounds, showing that a four-letter reversible alphabet reaches the static code-size orders in optimal quadratic and linear word length. In the fully dimension-limited regime, this yields \(\ln N_{\mathsf Q,4}=Θ(d^2)\) versus \(\ln N_{\mathsf S,4}=Θ(d)\), establishing a quadratic quantum--classical separation in logarithmic code size. Low-overlap Grassmann and agreement-code packings supply the orbit endpoints, while exact inverse query words match each encoded state to its designated test. At the sharp boundary \(λ_2=0\), \(0\leqλ_1<1\), all four model classes satisfy \(\ln N=Θ(\min\{\ln d,T\})\). Thus any fixed positive false-acceptance tolerance activates the metric-packing regime, whereas zero false acceptance imposes an exclusive-witness constraint and yields the logarithmic-dimension boundary.

AI.tldr: With only four shared, time-homogeneous generators, finite-horizon identification of a d-dimensional memory is possible with logarithmic code sizes Θ(min{d²,T}) for arbitrary CPTP generators and Θ(min{d,T}) for stochastic maps, attained by four unitary and four permutation letters respectively.
AI.motivation: The paper aims to determine finite-horizon identification limits of a d-dimensional memory when the control interface is restricted to only four shared, time-homogeneous generators, addressing how shared randomness plus a small generator alphabet constrain the achievable code sizes and whether reversible alphabets suffice.
AI.method: A writer applies a prefix word to a common root state; the verifier applies a candidate-dependent query word followed by a shared terminal binary test, each word of length at most T. Identification sizes are bounded for fixed error tolerances using low-overlap Grassmann packings and agreement-code packings for the orbit endpoints, with exact inverse query words matching encoded states to designated tests; four unitary and four permutation letters are constructed to realize the bounds.
AI.result: ln N_Q,4 = Θ(min{d²,T}) for arbitrary CPTP generators and ln N_S,4 = Θ(min{d,T}) for stochastic maps, both attained by four-letter reversible alphabets (unitary and permutation respectively). In the dimension-limited regime this gives ln N_Q,4 = Θ(d²) versus ln N_S,4 = Θ(d), a quadratic quantum–classical separation. At the sharp boundary λ₂=0, 0≤λ₁<1, all four model classes satisfy ln N = Θ(min{ln d, T}).
AI.conclusion: Any fixed positive false-acceptance tolerance activates the metric-packing regime and yields the static code-size orders, whereas zero false acceptance imposes an exclusive-witness constraint producing a logarithmic-dimension boundary. A four-letter reversible alphabet thus reaches optimal quadratic and linear word-length orders.

title: Three-axis Active Magnetic Compensation with Spatial Feedforward Matrix Decoupling and Hysteresis PI Regulation for Suppressing Zeeman Decoherence of Cold Atom Quantum Memories
summary: Cold-atom quantum memories require a near-zero magnetic environment (residual field <1 microtesla) to mitigate Zeeman decoherence. Conventional three-axis active compensation suffers from inter-coil crosstalk and geomagnetic drift, which degrade the uniformity and long-term stability of the zero-field region. To address this, we propose a spatiotemporally cooperative feedback-controlled suppression architecture for magnetic interference. An integrally printed three-dimensional orthogonal coil frame mechanically suppresses inter-axis flux leakage. A spatial feedforward inverse matrix is introduced to algorithmically eliminate first-order cross-coupling. A dual-threshold hysteresis incremental-PI controller filters magnetometer quantization fluctuations and avoids frequent small jitter adjustments of coil driving currents. Hardware ablation experiments, long-duration stability tests and spatial magnetic-field mapping were conducted. Experimental results show that during a 714.4 s continuous steady-hold stage, the mean and maximum residual fields at the central point reach 0.112 microtesla and 0.224 microtesla, respectively. The overlapping Allan deviations of all three components remain below 5 nT for averaging times of 1.9-178.2 s. Based on differential-ferrofluid lattice-scan measurements combined with centre-constrained quadratic vector reconstruction and soft Maxwell regularization, a weak-field spatial distribution with an RMS variation of 5.65 microtesla is fitted within a spherical region of interest of radius 5 mm, where 67.5% of the model volume meets the sub-5 microtesla coverage criterion. For a prolate ellipsoidal region matching the atomic-cloud distribution with full axis lengths of 10, 5, and 5 mm, the upper field bound within 93.7% of the volume is 2.68 microtesla.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a spatiotemporally cooperative feedback-controlled magnetic-field suppression architecture for cold-atom quantum memories, combining a printed 3D orthogonal coil frame, spatial feedforward inverse-matrix decoupling, and a dual-threshold hysteresis incremental-PI controller to achieve sub-microtesla stable zero-field conditions.
AI.motivation: Cold-atom quantum memories need a residual magnetic field below 1 µT to mitigate Zeeman decoherence, but conventional three-axis active compensation suffers from inter-coil crosstalk and geomagnetic drift, degrading the uniformity and long-term stability of the zero-field region.
AI.method: The proposed architecture integrates three elements: (1) an integrally printed three-dimensional orthogonal coil frame that mechanically suppresses inter-axis flux leakage; (2) a spatial feedforward inverse matrix that algorithmically eliminates first-order cross-coupling; and (3) a dual-threshold hysteresis incremental-PI controller that filters magnetometer quantization fluctuations and avoids frequent small jitter adjustments of coil currents. Validation includes hardware ablation experiments, long-duration stability tests, and spatial magnetic-field mapping using differential-ferrofluid lattice-scan measurements with centre-constrained quadratic vector reconstruction and soft Maxwell regularization.
AI.result: During a 714.4 s steady-hold stage, the mean and maximum residual fields at the central point were 0.112 µT and 0.224 µT. Overlapping Allan deviations of all three components stayed below 5 nT for averaging times of 1.9–178.2 s. A weak-field distribution with 5.65 µT RMS variation was fitted within a 5 mm-radius spherical region of interest, with 67.5% of the model volume meeting the sub-5 µT coverage criterion; for a prolate ellipsoid (10 × 5 × 5 mm) matching the atomic cloud, the field bound within 93.7% of the volume was 2.68 µT.
AI.conclusion: The spatiotemporally cooperative feedback architecture effectively suppresses magnetic interference and achieves high uniformity and long-term stability of the zero-field region, providing a viable magnetic environment for cold-atom quantum memories by meeting the sub-microtesla central residual requirement and offering good spatial coverage over the atomic-cloud volume.

title: Superconducting circuits host two-level systems with lifetimes exceeding one second
summary: Understanding the microscopic environment of superconducting qubits is a central challenge for quantum technologies. Parasitic two-level systems (TLSs) of various microscopic origins are ubiquitous and limit qubit performance through decoherence, frequency drifts, and leakage. Recently, long-lived TLSs with lifetimes exceeding those of state-of-the-art qubits have been shown to induce correlated qubit dynamics, with direct implications for quantum error correction. Here, we perform wide-band quantum-jump correlation spectroscopy on flux-tunable transmon qubits and identify microscopic degrees of freedom that outlive the qubit by orders of magnitude. Pump-probe measurements at varying detunings from these objects reveal intrinsic lifetimes exceeding one second. Their weak coupling to the qubit, in the kilohertz range, is consistent with positional defects described by the standard tunneling model, without excluding other microscopic origins such as magnetic spin impurities or trapped quasiparticles. More broadly, these results establish superconducting qubits as a sensitive probe of exceptionally long-lived microscopic degrees of freedom and open a route toward their controlled access and functionalization.

AI.tldr: Wide-band quantum-jump correlation spectroscopy on flux-tunable transmons reveals microscopic two-level degrees of freedom with intrinsic lifetimes exceeding one second—orders of magnitude longer than the qubits themselves—weakly coupled at kilohertz rates.
AI.motivation: Parasitic two-level systems (TLSs) limit superconducting qubit performance via decoherence, frequency drift, and leakage; recent evidence that long-lived TLSs induce correlated qubit dynamics matters critically for quantum error correction, so the microscopic origin and lifetime of these fluctuators must be characterized.
AI.method: Wide-band quantum-jump correlation spectroscopy on flux-tunable transmon qubits, combined with pump-probe measurements at varying detunings from the detected fluctuators.
AI.result: Identified microscopic degrees of freedom outliving the qubit by orders of magnitude, with intrinsic lifetimes exceeding one second and weak qubit coupling in the kilohertz range, consistent with positional defects in the standard tunneling model (without excluding magnetic spin impurities or trapped quasiparticles).
AI.conclusion: Superconducting qubits serve as sensitive probes of exceptionally long-lived microscopic degrees of freedom, opening routes toward their controlled access and functionalization; the coexistence of ultralong-lived TLSs with high-performance qubits has direct implications for correlated noise and error correction.

title: Hybrid Quantum-Classical Optimization for Emergency-Priority Traffic Signal Control
summary: Emergency-priority traffic signal control requires reducing emergency-vehicle delay while limiting disruption to ordinary traffic. This work investigates a finite-horizon QUBO formulation and compares Exact QUBO optimization, QAOA, CVaR-QAOA, a quantum machine-learning policy, fixed-time control, and max-pressure control in a three-intersection corridor. The study evaluates three traffic-demand regimes, examines the effect of the emergency-priority weight, and compares quantum solutions with the exact QUBO optimum. The optimization-based controllers achieved reliable emergency progression across all tested demand regimes, while max-pressure produced lower ordinary-traffic delay. Increasing emergency priority reduced emergency travel time but increased congestion, with diminishing improvements at larger weights. CVaR-QAOA reproduced the exact QUBO solution more accurately than standard QAOA, although the resulting differences in closed-loop traffic performance were comparatively small.

AI.tldr: A finite-horizon QUBO formulation for emergency-priority traffic signal control is benchmarked across quantum (Exact QUBO, QAOA, CVaR-QAOA, quantum-ML policy) and classical (fixed-time, max-pressure) controllers in a three-intersection corridor, examining demand regimes and emergency-priority weight.
AI.motivation: Emergency-priority signal control must minimize emergency-vehicle delay without excessively disrupting ordinary traffic, motivating a formal optimization formulation and a systematic comparison of quantum and classical control strategies.
AI.method: A finite-horizon QUBO formulation of the signal-control problem is solved via Exact QUBO optimization, standard QAOA, CVaR-QAOA, and a quantum machine-learning policy, and compared against fixed-time and max-pressure controllers in a simulated three-intersection corridor under three traffic-demand regimes; the emergency-priority weight is varied, and quantum solutions are compared to the exact QUBO optimum.
AI.result: Optimization-based controllers achieved reliable emergency progression across all demand regimes, whereas max-pressure yielded lower ordinary-traffic delay. Increasing the emergency-priority weight reduced emergency travel time but raised congestion, with diminishing returns at larger weights. CVaR-QAOA reproduced the exact QUBO solution more accurately than standard QAOA, though the resulting closed-loop traffic-performance differences were relatively small.
AI.conclusion: The QUBO-based approach reliably prioritizes emergency vehicles, and CVaR-QAOA offers improved solution fidelity over standard QAOA, but these accuracy gains translate into only modest closed-loop performance differences; a trade-off between emergency priority and ordinary-traffic delay persists.

title: Selected Stabilizer Subspaces for Compact Many-Body Wave Functions
summary: Selected configuration interaction (SCI) obtains accurate many-body solutions by variationally diagonalising the Hamiltonian in a sparse, iteratively selected set of configurations, but can lose compactness when the target state has broad configurational support. We introduce selected stabilizer interaction (SSI), a fully classical, SCI-inspired method that instead iteratively constructs a nonorthogonal subspace spanned by a systematically enlargeable set of selected stabilizer states. A single stabilizer, generated by Clifford operations, can encode a structured superposition of (possibly exponentially) many configurations, shifting the relevant compression from configurational to stabilizer sparsity. We benchmark ground-state energies, fidelities, superposition degrees and required expansion lengths against exact diagonalization and equivalent SCI schemes for the transverse-field Ising, XXZ Heisenberg, and Hubbard models, finding particularly strong compression from the stabilizer representation in the spin models, and increasing advantage with system size for these systems. The results establish a proof of principle for heuristic selected stabilizer diagonalization, while also identifying particular challenges in symmetry handling and effective exploration of the stabilizer space.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces selected stabilizer interaction (SSI), a fully classical, SCI-inspired method that iteratively builds a nonorthogonal subspace of selected stabilizer states to compress many-body ground states by shifting compression from configurations to stabilizers.
AI.motivation: Selected configuration interaction (SCI) yields accurate many-body solutions but loses compactness when the target state has broad configurational support. The authors aim to overcome this by exploiting the ability of a single stabilizer state (generated by Clifford operations) to encode a structured superposition of potentially exponentially many configurations.
AI.method: SSI iteratively constructs a nonorthogonal subspace spanned by a systematically enlargeable set of selected stabilizer states, retaining the SCI variational philosophy but replacing configurations with stabilizer states so that compression shifts from configurational to stabilizer sparsity. It is benchmarked against exact diagonalization and equivalent SCI schemes on the transverse-field Ising, XXZ Heisenberg, and Hubbard models, reporting ground-state energies, fidelities, superposition degrees, and required expansion lengths.
AI.result: SSI shows particularly strong compression from the stabilizer representation in the spin models, with the advantage increasing with system size for those systems. Competitive accuracy is obtained in energies and fidelities relative to exact diagonalization and SCI baselines.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a proof of principle for heuristic selected stabilizer diagonalization, while identifying outstanding challenges in symmetry handling and effective exploration of the stabilizer space.

title: Looking Beyond Visibility: Resolving the Temporal Structure of Continuous-Wave Four-Photon Hong-Ou-Mandel Interference
summary: Hong-Ou-Mandel interference underpins many photonic quantum information protocols and is commonly characterized by a single visibility parameter. This quantity is typically obtained by averaging over a fixed coincidence window, thereby discarding details of the underlying temporal structure that are critical in continuous-wave processes. Four-photon interference with continuous-wave sources furthermore requires photon pairs with long coherence times, which we generate in microring resonators and measure with ultrafast time-resolved detection.
