Here, we model and resolve their interference and temporal structure by recording all four photon arrival times and mapping their relative delays onto a three-dimensional coincidence histogram relative to a trigger detection. The resulting structure preserves relative arrival-time correlations that are usually discarded and enables post-processed optimization of coincidence windows to trade off visibility against count rate. This method provides a general benchmark for continuous-wave sources in interference-based quantum network protocols.

AI.tldr: The authors resolve four-photon Hong-Ou-Mandel interference from continuous-wave microring resonators by recording all photon arrival times and building a three-dimensional coincidence histogram of relative delays, revealing discarded temporal correlations and enabling post-processed window optimization of visibility versus count rate.
AI.motivation: Conventional HOM interferometry is summarized by a single visibility averaged over a fixed coincidence window, which discards the temporal structure essential to continuous-wave sources; four-photon interference with CW pumps additionally demands long-coherence photon pairs, and existing characterizations provide no general benchmark capturing these dynamics.
AI.method: Photon pairs with long coherence times are generated in microring resonators and measured with ultrafast time-resolved detection. All four photon arrival times are recorded relative to a trigger detection and mapped into a three-dimensional coincidence histogram, yielding a model and full resolution of the interference and temporal structure.
AI.result: The three-dimensional histogram preserves relative arrival-time correlations normally averaged away, and it supports post-processed optimization of coincidence windows that trades off visibility against count rate.
AI.conclusion: Time-resolved multi-photon coincidence mapping offers a general benchmark for continuous-wave sources in interference-based quantum network protocols, superseding single-visibility characterization.

title: Opinion bubbles in the quantum Buridan's ass problem
summary: The quantum Buridan's ass problem concerns a network of interconnected nodes in which transitions between the nodes are governed by the laws of quantum mechanics. In such situations interference between probability amplitudes plays a key role in determining whether the probability of leaving the initial node is large or small and also the speed at which the associated transitions occur. In this paper we extend this idea to consider transitions between one given set of coupled nodes and the remainder of the network. We have in mind a quantum analogy to changing an opinion, in which the initially occupied set of nodes is one opinion bubble, with the remaining parts of the network corresponding to a different opinion. We find that quantum interference again plays a crucial role in the dynamics. A further key component is the role of symmetry between the nodes and their interconnections, as it is symmetry that lies at the heart of the Buridan's ass puzzle. In the classical Buridan's ass paradox it is symmetry between competing alternatives that freezes the ass into indecision. In the quantum case, however, interference results in a far richer dynamics.

AI.tldr: The paper extends the quantum Buridan's ass problem from single-node transitions to transitions between a set of coupled nodes ("opinion bubble") and the rest of the network, modeling opinion change via quantum interference and node symmetry.
AI.motivation: Classical Buridan's ass freezes under symmetry between competing alternatives; the authors want a quantum analogue where interference produces richer dynamics, framed as an analogy to changing an opinion between an initial set of nodes and the remainder of a network.
AI.method: Analysis of quantum dynamics on an interconnected node network, treating transitions between a designated coupled subset of nodes and the complementary network, examining probability amplitudes, interference effects on transition speed, and the role of symmetry among nodes and interconnections.
AI.result: Quantum interference is found to play a crucial role in the dynamics of transitions between the node subset and the remainder; symmetry among nodes and their couplings also emerges as a key determinant of the behavior.
AI.conclusion: Whereas classical symmetry induces indecision/freezing, quantum interference yields substantially richer transition dynamics, supporting the opinion-change analogy within a quantum network framework.

title: Synergistic charging of a quantum battery via Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction and non-Markovian noise
comment: 12 pages, 13 figures. Accepted by Physical Review A, comments are welcome
summary: Protecting quantum batteries from environmental noise remains a challenge. Using exact Burshtein-Kubo equations, we study a two-spin quantum battery with Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya (DM) coupling under indepen dent local longitudinal random telegraph noise (RTN). At a fixed effective noise scale, the DM-assisted slow switching protocol yields a superadditive transient ergotropy gain and near-maximal ergotropy during the initial charging stage, while the no-DM slow-switching control reaches comparable ergotropy only in a later revival. A finite superadditive region persists at fixed RTN amplitude, with protocol-dependent location and gain. In the Ising model, the enhancement is nonmonotonic in DM strength, with intermediate coupling giving near-optimal performance. Dressed-channel analysis associates this enhancement with changes in transition frequencies and longitudinal-noise matrix elements that reduce slow-RTN spectral weight. Superadditivity also persists in the tested anisotropic XY model.

AI.tldr: DM coupling plus slow RTN switching yields superadditive transient ergotropy in a two-spin quantum battery, driven by dressed-channel spectral-weight redistribution.
AI.motivation: Protecting quantum batteries from environmental noise remains an open challenge; the work asks whether Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya coupling can counter decoherence-driven ergotropy loss under local longitudinal random telegraph noise.
AI.method: Exact Burshtein-Kubo equations are used to model a two-spin quantum battery with DM coupling under independent local longitudinal RTN. Ergotropy is compared across DM-assisted versus no-DM slow-switching protocols at fixed effective noise scale, with dressed-channel analysis of transition frequencies and longitudinal-noise matrix elements; robustness is tested in Ising and anisotropic XY models.
AI.result: At fixed effective noise scale, DM-assisted slow switching produces a superadditive transient ergotropy gain and near-maximal ergotropy in the initial charging stage, whereas the no-DM control reaches comparable ergotropy only in a later revival. A finite superadditive region persists at fixed RTN amplitude with protocol-dependent location and gain. In the Ising model the enhancement is nonmonotonic in DM strength, with intermediate coupling near-optimal; superadditivity also survives in the anisotropic XY model.
AI.conclusion: DM coupling can enhance and accelerate ergotropy extraction from a two-spin quantum battery under slow longitudinal RTN, with the benefit traced to reduced slow-RTN spectral weight via shifted transition frequencies and modified noise matrix elements, and it generalizes across tested spin models.

title: ZZ-Free bSWAP Gates under Strong Driving in Far-Detuned Fixed-Frequency Transmons
summary: Far-detuned frequency allocations in fixed-frequency superconducting processors mitigate spectral crowding but constrain cross-resonance interactions at practical drive amplitudes. Here, we demonstrate that a single strong drive induces a large $XX-YY$ interaction in the far-detuned regime, while a weak second tone tunes the accompanying $ZZ$ phase. The interaction realizes a 150-ns $\sqrt{\mathrm{bSWAP}}$ gate, which can directly prepare a maximally entangled state from the ground state. For the implementations on the same qubit pair at matched drive strengths, cross resonance gives a shorter CNOT operation, while $\sqrt{\mathrm{bSWAP}}$ gives a 33% shorter SWAP operation with a higher IRB fidelity. The multilevel theory further predicts a regime where stronger driving can yield a speed advantage for CNOT as well, a possibility absent in the two-level model. As an application of the $XX-YY$ interaction, we also demonstrate two-spin squeezing beyond the standard quantum limit through two-axis countertwisting. The interaction realized here complements cross resonance and offers a route to efficient gate synthesis and quantum simulation of interacting spin systems.

AI.tldr: A single strong drive generates a large XX-YY interaction in far-detuned superconducting qubits, with a weak second tone tuning the residual ZZ phase, enabling a 150-ns sqrt(bSWAP) gate and two-spin squeezing beyond the standard quantum limit.
AI.motivation: Far-detuned frequency allocations in fixed-frequency superconducting processors reduce spectral crowding but weaken cross-resonance interactions at practical drive amplitudes, limiting gate options in this regime.
AI.method: Apply one strong microwave drive to induce a large XX-YY interaction in the far-detuned regime, combined with a weak second tone to tune the accompanying ZZ phase; characterize the interaction via multilevel theory and benchmark gates on the same qubit pair against cross resonance at matched drive strengths.
AI.result: Realizes a 150-ns sqrt(bSWAP) gate that directly prepares a maximally entangled state from the ground state; versus cross resonance at matched drive, CNOT is shorter with cross resonance while sqrt(bSWAP) yields a 33% shorter SWAP with higher IRB fidelity; multilevel theory predicts a regime where stronger driving can also give CNOT a speed advantage (absent in the two-level model); two-spin squeezing beyond the standard quantum limit is demonstrated via two-axis countertwisting.
AI.conclusion: The drive-induced XX-YY interaction complements cross resonance, offering a route to efficient gate synthesis and quantum simulation of interacting spin systems in fixed-frequency far-detuned processors.

title: Quantum control of solid state qubits via Reinforcement Learning
summary: The use of reinforcement learning (RL) in the design of quantum control strategies for pulse level control of NISQ era quantum devices is attracting growing interest. Model-free RL, not requiring preexisting knowledge of the physical system, acts as a black-box optimization tool well suited for noisy devices. In this work, we provide a simulation-based analysis of the performance of model-free RL for state preparation and qubit gate design in a challenging setup: indirect control of NV nuclear spins in a spin-bath. In particular, the spin-bath is modeled via the generalized cluster correlation expansion accounting for magnetic impurities and intra-bath interactions. We analyze the performance of the RL agents by performing simulations with minimally observable environments and noisy, sparse rewards as introduced in (Phys. Rev. X 12, 011059), and compare them to other state-of-the-art black-box optimization tools.

AI.tldr: This work simulates model-free reinforcement learning (RL) for pulse-level state preparation and gate design on indirectly controlled NV-center nuclear spins in a spin bath, comparing RL agents to other black-box optimizers under sparse, noisy rewards and minimal observability.
AI.motivation: RL is gaining traction for pulse-level control of NISQ devices because model-free, black-box optimization needs no prior system knowledge and suits noisy hardware. However, its value in a demanding setting—indirect control of NV nuclear spins interacting with a magnetic-impurity spin bath—remains unclear, motivating a simulation-based benchmark.
AI.method: Simulation-based study: the spin bath is modeled via generalized cluster correlation expansion (gCCE), capturing magnetic impurities and intra-bath interactions. RL agents are trained for state preparation and qubit gate design under minimally observable environments and noisy, sparse rewards (following Phys. Rev. X 12, 011059), then benchmarked against state-of-the-art black-box optimization methods.
AI.result: The abstract reports a comparative performance analysis of model-free RL agents versus other state-of-the-art black-box optimizers in this challenging indirect-control, spin-bath setting, with the gCCE bath model providing the simulation testbed.
AI.conclusion: Model-free RL is evaluated as a black-box tool for pulse-level quantum control under realistic noise and limited observability; the study positions RL relative to established optimizers for NV nuclear-spin state preparation and gate design.

title: Thermal activation of photon catalysis in difference-intensity Mach-Zehnder interferometry with squeezed thermal light
summary: Realistic non-Gaussian operations, which can be implemented by mixing a nonclassical Gaussian state with a Fock state at a beam splitter and then heralding on a photon-number-resolving detector, are known to improve phase estimation in a Mach-Zehnder interferometer. The existing studies have considered the single-mode squeezed vacuum for difference-intensity and parity detection, and the two-mode squeezed thermal state for parity detection alone as the initial Gaussian resources. However, a real squeezer in the lab actually produces single-mode squeezed thermal light, which has not been studied in a coherent-plus-resource interferometer. We take up this case and using the phase space Wigner picture, we obtain the heralded state produced by photon subtraction, addition and catalysis on a single-mode squeezed thermal resource, and evaluate the corresponding phase sensitivities. Single-photon catalysis, which is useless on squeezed vacuum, becomes a useful operation for any thermal occupation above $\nth\simeq0.2$, and since it heralds with a probability near one-half, it turns out to be the best success-weighted operation over the whole thermal range. In the vacuum limit our results reproduce the known hierarchy, where two-photon catalysis is the best operation. The quantum Fisher information computations confirms that thermal noise enhances the phase information encoded in the catalyzed state, demonstrating that difference-intensity detection closely approaches the ultimate precision bound across most operational regimes, and, together with a loss analysis, verifies the robustness of the effect.

AI.tldr: Realistic non-Gaussian operations (photon subtraction, addition, and catalysis) applied to single-mode squeezed thermal light are analyzed in a coherent-plus-resource Mach-Zehnder interferometer. Single-photon catalysis, useless for squeezed vacuum, becomes optimal for thermal occupation above nth≈0.2 and is the best success-weighted operation across the entire thermal range, with difference-intensity detection nearly reaching the quantum Fisher information bound.
AI.motivation: Prior studies of non-Gaussian-enhanced phase estimation used idealized Gaussian resources: single-mode squeezed vacuum (for difference-intensity and parity detection) and two-mode squeezed thermal states (for parity detection only). However, a real laboratory squeezer produces single-mode squeezed thermal light, a resource that has not been examined in a coherent-plus-resource interferometer. This gap motivates assessing realistic thermal contamination.
AI.method: The authors use the phase-space Wigner picture to derive the heralded output states produced by photon subtraction, photon addition, and photon catalysis (single- and two-photon) acting on a single-mode squeezed thermal state at a beam splitter, heralded by a photon-number-resolving detector. They then evaluate the corresponding phase sensitivities for the resulting interferometric scheme, computing both classical-estimator sensitivities and the quantum Fisher information, and perform a loss analysis to test robustness.
AI.result: Single-photon catalysis, which is ineffective on squeezed vacuum, becomes a useful operation for any thermal occupation above nth≈0.2; because it heralds with probability near one-half, it is the best success-weighted operation over the whole thermal range. In the vacuum limit, the known hierarchy is recovered, with two-photon catalysis being the best operation. Quantum Fisher information calculations show that thermal noise enhances the phase information encoded in the catalyzed state. Difference-intensity detection closely approaches the ultimate precision bound across most operational regimes, and the loss analysis confirms the robustness of the effect.
AI.conclusion: Realistic squeezed thermal resources, rather than idealized squeezed vacuum, alter which non-Gaussian operation is optimal: single-photon catalysis dominates under realistic thermal occupation due to its high heralding probability and noise-enhanced phase information. Difference-intensity detection is a near-optimal practical measurement, and the advantage persists under loss, supporting the feasibility of these schemes with real squeezers.

title: Loss-independent time-delay estimation via Hong-Ou-Mandel photon bunching detection
summary: In this work we study the application of two-photon correlated quantum states for high-precision time estimation. To achieve this, photon pairs were fed into a Hong-Ou-Mandel polarization interferometer to generate N00N entangled states with $N = 2$. Two- and four-detector schemes were considered, and the achievable time estimation precision of each was studied, with particular emphasis on the system's Fisher information in each case. Our results reveal that using a four-detector scheme, enabling the measurement of both coincidence and photon-bunching terms, achieves the maximum precision given by the quantum Fisher information, without the need of characterizing system losses. We also show that correlations between repetitions arise due to systematic errors, limiting the precision enhancement that can be obtained by increasing the number of repetitions. Taking these correlations into account, we show that the four-detector scheme outperforms the two-detector scheme in the precision of time-delay estimation. With the experimentally determined calibration uncertainties, the four-detector scheme improves the dispersion by a factor of 2 for the repetitions performed, reaching up to a factor of 4 as both schemes approach their systematic floors.

AI.tldr: Two-photon N00N states (N=2) in a HOM polarization interferometer enable time estimation reaching the quantum Fisher information bound using a four-detector scheme that requires no loss characterization; accounting for repetition correlations from systematic errors, this scheme outperforms the two-detector approach.
AI.motivation: High-precision time estimation benefits from quantum-enhanced metrology. The authors aim to determine whether correlated two-photon states, and specifically which detection architecture, can extract maximum precision in time-delay estimation while being robust to system losses and systematic errors.
AI.method: Photon pairs are injected into a Hong-Ou-Mandel polarization interferometer to generate N00N entangled states with N=2. Two- and four-detector measurement schemes are analyzed, computing the achievable precision via Fisher information. The four-detector scheme measures both coincidence and photon-bunching terms. Repetition-to-repetition correlations induced by systematic errors are modeled, and experiments with calibrated uncertainties are performed.
AI.result: The four-detector scheme attains the maximum precision set by the quantum Fisher information without needing to characterize system losses. Systematic errors create correlations between repetitions that cap the precision gain from increasing repetition count. With experimentally determined calibration uncertainties, the four-detector scheme improves dispersion by a factor of 2 for the repetitions performed, reaching up to a factor of 4 as both schemes approach their systematic floors.
AI.conclusion: A four-detector HOM-based scheme with two-photon N00N states provides loss-robust, quantum-Fisher-information-limited time-delay estimation and outperforms the two-detector scheme, with systematic-error-induced correlations representing the dominant practical limit on precision enhancement.

title: Energetic channels in finite many-body quantum charging
summary: We examine how a finite many-body system can function as an effective charger for a single-qubit quantum battery, using the Lipkin-Meshkov-Glick model as a paradigmatic setting. As our figure of merit, we consider the battery ergotropy while explicitly resolving the energetic flows across the composite system. In the absence of intra-charger interactions, we show that the generation of non-zero ergotropy is controlled by the competition between collective coupling and spectral mismatch. We further demonstrate that even passive positive-temperature charger states can generate finite battery ergotropy, provided the charger is sufficiently large and sufficiently hot. Intra-charger interactions restructure the charger spectrum and qualitatively modify the available energetic pathways. While they can enhance the amount of energy accessible for charging, they can simultaneously divert energy into internal many-body and battery-charger interaction channels, producing an energetic impedance to direct charger-to-battery transfer. Consequently, battery ergotropy alone is insufficient to characterize an effective many-body charger: the useful work generated and its energetic provenance must be assessed together.

AI.tldr: Using the Lipkin-Meshkov-Glick model, the paper studies a finite many-body system as a charger for a single-qubit quantum battery, tracking ergotropy together with explicit energetic flows. It shows ergotropy generation is governed by collective coupling versus spectral mismatch, that hot and large passive chargers can still charge the battery, and that intra-charger interactions, while boosting accessible energy, can divert energy into internal many-body and interaction channels, creating an "energetic impedance" to direct transfer.
AI.motivation: Many-body systems are promising chargers for quantum batteries, but battery ergotropy alone is an incomplete figure of merit: energy may be stored or diverted in internal charger and interaction channels rather than delivered as useful work. The paper motivates a combined energetic-accounting approach that resolves where the energy actually goes during charging.
AI.method: The Lipkin-Meshkov-Glick model is used as a paradigmatic finite many-body charger coupled to a single-qubit battery. The figure of merit is battery ergotropy, computed while explicitly resolving energetic flows across the composite charger-battery system. The analysis is performed first without intra-charger interactions (competition of collective coupling and spectral mismatch; passive positive-temperature charger states) and then with intra-charger interactions (restructured charger spectrum and modified energetic pathways).
AI.result: Without intra-charger interactions, non-zero ergotropy arises from the competition between collective coupling and spectral mismatch, and passive positive-temperature charger states can generate finite battery ergotropy if the charger is sufficiently large and hot. Intra-charger interactions restructure the charger spectrum and qualitatively change the available energetic pathways: they can increase the energy accessible for charging while simultaneously diverting energy into internal many-body and battery-charger interaction channels, producing an energetic impedance to direct charger-to-battery transfer.
AI.conclusion: Battery ergotropy alone is insufficient to characterize an effective many-body charger; the useful work generated and its energetic provenance must be assessed together. Effective charging requires that energy flow through the intended charger-to-battery channel rather than being trapped in internal many-body or interaction degrees of freedom.

title: Generalized $m$-body mean-field projections for classical simulation of $d$-dimensional Heisenberg-picture dynamics
comment: Companion paper to arXiv:2609.12840; 35 pages; 6 figures; supplementary numerical results and analytical proofs included. Comments and suggestions are appreciated
summary: Classical simulation of quantum many-body dynamics is challenged by the rapid growth of operator complexity, particularly in higher dimensions where tensor-network methods become increasingly demanding. We develop state-adapted Pauli-weight propagation based on generalized $m$-body mean-field projections, which compress many-body observables into optimal low-body representations in a covariance geometry induced by the initial state. Combined with adaptive Krylov-like restricted Heisenberg dynamics, this provides an alternative to conventional Hilbert--Schmidt Pauli-weight truncation. We derive necessary and conditional sufficient bounds on low-body approximation accuracy using standard operator complexity measures and characterize possible dynamical failure mechanisms of the state-adapted method. Numerical benchmarks demonstrate substantial state-dependent accuracy gains, while identifying regimes of reduced accuracy or violations of Pauli spectral bounds. For a three-dimensional system of $80$ interacting spins, our method achieves strong body-order convergence, close agreement with independently converging tensor-network simulations, and substantially smaller sparse Pauli representations. These results establish state-adapted Pauli propagation as a promising approach to classical simulation of higher-dimensional coherent many-body dynamics.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces "state-adapted Pauli-weight propagation" using generalized m-body mean-field projections in a covariance geometry set by the initial state, combined with Krylov-like restricted Heisenberg dynamics, as an alternative to Hilbert–Schmidt Pauli-weight truncation for classically simulating higher-dimensional quantum many-body dynamics.
AI.motivation: Classical simulation of quantum many-body dynamics is limited by rapid growth of operator complexity; in higher dimensions tensor-network methods become increasingly demanding, and conventional Hilbert–Schmidt Pauli-weight truncation ignores the structure of the initial state.
AI.method: Many-body observables are compressed into optimal low-body representations via generalized m-body mean-field projections in a covariance geometry induced by the initial state, combined with adaptive Krylov-like restricted Heisenberg dynamics. The authors derive necessary and conditional sufficient bounds on low-body approximation accuracy using standard operator complexity measures and characterize dynamical failure mechanisms of the state-adapted scheme.
AI.result: Numerical benchmarks show substantial state-dependent accuracy gains, along with identified regimes of reduced accuracy or violations of Pauli spectral bounds. For a three-dimensional system of 80 interacting spins, the method achieves strong body-order convergence, close agreement with independently converging tensor-network simulations, and substantially smaller sparse Pauli representations.
AI.conclusion: State-adapted Pauli propagation is established as a promising approach for classical simulation of higher-dimensional coherent many-body dynamics.

title: Bubble-Sort Exchange Networks: Symmetry Selection Rules and Language-Model Distillation on Exchange-Only Spin Chains
comment: 19 pages, 9 figures, 7 tables. Code and data: https://github.com/minatoyuichiro/eoall-check
summary: On a chain of exchange-coupled quantum dots a Heisenberg exchange pulse of area pi is a SWAP, so the parallel bubble-sort SWAP network of superconducting chains is native to exchange-only (EO) spin qubits, and any other pulse area fuses routing with an entangling interaction. We build a variational "bubble-sort exchange network" (odd-even transposition, one parameter per pulse) and study it as a Born machine read out by Pauli spin blockade. Exchange conserves total spin, so the reachable readout distributions are fixed by the total-spin content of the initial product state. For the two-spin singlet-triplet encoding we derive a selection rule -- outcomes with k triplet pairs are bounded by the initial weight in sectors S <= k (S = 0 excluded for k = 1) -- and prove by a transportation argument that it is also sufficient: the reachable distributions form the polytope cut out by the rule, and its total-variation floor is attained. Products of singlets and T0's forbid whole outcome classes; the Neel state forbids none; the three-spin EO code has no floor. We then distil, in noise-free simulation, next-token distributions of GPT-2 over restricted vocabularies into the network, with matrix-product-state (MPS) Born machines as classical control. At six logical qubits the three-spin chain reaches KL = 0.011 nat at depth N and 0.004 at 2N, below the bond-dimension-4 MPS; the two-spin chain from the Neel state reaches 0.014 at 2N and 0.004 at 3N, against 0.28-1.5 from singlet/triplet products for the first teacher. Final states lie largely outside the code space: leakage is a resource, not an error. No arrangement of disjoint pulses meets every pair in fewer than N-1 rounds, and at depth 2N the chain distils as well as a 2D array or non-local couplings. Sector-restricted simulation extends this to 10-14 logical qubits (up to 30 dots).

AI.tldr: A variational "bubble-sort exchange network" (odd-even transposition with one parameter per Heisenberg exchange pulse) on chain-coupled quantum dots is studied as a Born machine and used to distil restricted-vocabulary GPT-2 next-token distributions, reaching KL values as low as 0.004 nat and beating bond-dimension-4 MPS controls.
AI.motivation: Native hardware structure: on a chain of exchange-coupled quantum dots, a pi-area Heisenberg exchange pulse is exactly a SWAP, so the parallel bubble-sort SWAP network of superconducting chains is the natural primitive for exchange-only (EO) spin qubits; the authors want to exploit this native routing and ask whether such a pulse network can serve as an expressive variational Born machine for generative modelling.
AI.method: Build a variational odd-even transposition ("bubble-sort") exchange network with one variational parameter per pulse, read out by Pauli spin blockade. Analyse reachability: since exchange conserves total spin, reachable readout distributions are constrained by the total-spin content of the initial product state. For the two-spin singlet-triplet encoding, derive a selection rule (outcomes with k triplet pairs bounded by initial weight in sectors S <= k, with S = 0 excluded for k = 1) and prove sufficiency via a transportation argument, characterising the reachable set as a polytope whose total-variation floor is attained. Specific initial states (products of singlets and T0, the Neel state, the three-spin EO code) are analysed. The network is then trained, in noise-free simulation, to distil next-token distributions of GPT-2 on restricted vocabularies, with MPS Born machines as classical controls; sector-restricted simulation scales to 10-14 logical qubits.
AI.result: At six logical qubits, the three-spin chain reaches KL = 0.011 nat at depth N and 0.004 at 2N, below a bond-dimension-4 MPS; the two-spin chain initialised in the Neel state reaches 0.014 at 2N and 0.004 at 3N, versus 0.28-1.5 for singlet/triplet products. Final states lie largely outside the code space, showing leakage acts as a resource rather than an error. No arrangement of disjoint pulses meets every pair in fewer than N-1 rounds, and at depth 2N the chain matches a 2D array or non-local couplings. Sector-restricted simulation extends results to 10-14 logical qubits (up to 30 dots).
AI.conclusion: The parallel bubble-sort exchange network is a native, expressive and provably characterisable Born machine for EO spin qubits: reachable distributions are exactly the polytope cut out by a total-spin selection rule, the TV floor is attained, and the network distils GPT-2 next-token distributions to low KL, outperforming MPS controls. Code-space leakage is beneficial, chain topology suffices relative to 2D/non-local couplings, and sector-restricted simulation scales the scheme to 10-14 logical qubits.

title: Operational Limits of Gravity-Mediated Entanglement
summary: Tests of gravity-mediated entanglement aim to determine whether two massive objects in spatial superposition can become entangled through their mutual gravitational interaction. In an ideal model, the two objects are often treated as pointlike branches, but real wave packets have a finite width and are also exposed to dephasing and residual non-gravitational forces. We study these effects in a two-branch gravitational cat-state model with Gaussian wave packets. The Newtonian interaction is averaged over the finite wave-packet width, and spatially correlated dephasing is included phenomenologically. We then ask a practical question: when does the generated state remain useful rather than merely entangled? To answer this, we examine Bell violation, teleportation fidelity, coherent information, Fisher information, and state distinguishability. We find finite parameter windows where the same state is Bell-nonlocal and teleportation-useful, but these windows shrink as the wave packets become broader or the dephasing becomes stronger. We also show that a residual electrostatic branch interaction can coherently cancel the gravitational nonlocal phase and strongly suppress the operational signal. The results identify finite-width and electrostatic tolerance boundaries that should be considered in future tests of gravity-mediated entanglement.

AI.tldr: Finite wave-packet width and correlated dephasing reduce the operational usefulness of gravity-mediated entanglement; residual electrostatic interactions can cancel the gravitational phase and suppress signals. Finite tolerance windows remain for Bell nonlocality and teleportation.
AI.motivation: Ideal treatments of gravity-mediated entanglement assume pointlike branches, ignoring finite wave-packet width, dephasing, and residual non-gravitational forces that afflict real experiments. The authors ask not merely when entanglement appears, but when the generated state remains operationally useful.
AI.method: A two-branch gravitational cat-state model with Gaussian wave packets is analyzed: the Newtonian interaction is averaged over finite wave-packet width, and spatially correlated dephasing is added phenomenologically. Operational diagnostics include Bell violation, teleportation fidelity, coherent information, Fisher information, and state distinguishability, plus a residual electrostatic branch interaction.
AI.result: Finite parameter windows exist where the state is simultaneously Bell-nonlocal and teleportation-useful, but these windows shrink with broader wave packets or stronger dephasing. A residual electrostatic branch interaction can coherently cancel the gravitational nonlocal phase, strongly suppressing the operational signal.
AI.conclusion: The study identifies finite-width and electrostatic tolerance boundaries that provide practical criteria for future tests of gravity-mediated entanglement, showing entanglement alone is insufficient for usefulness.

title: Patchwork: automated lattice surgery and space-time partitioning for real-time decoding
summary: We introduce patchwork, a lattice-surgery compiler for arbitrary multi-qubit Pauli measurements on a prescribed narrow-corridor two-dimensional surface-code layout. Systematic geometric rules simplify stabilizer placement and gate scheduling, including for logical $Y$ measurements implemented using twist defects. We introduce measurement circuits and schedules that, together with protruding lobes of $Y$-extension patches, preserve the full effective code distance for all numerically tested code distances. To support parallel decoding, we develop a wavefront algorithm that partitions merged lattice-surgery patches into space-time commit, buffer, and cleanup regions. Simulations of three sequential multi-qubit Pauli measurements acting on ten logical qubits show that staged decoding achieves total failure probabilities close to those of monolithic decoding over the parameters tested. These methods provide an automated framework for fault-tolerant lattice surgery and a route toward scalable, real-time decoding.

AI.tldr: Patchwork is an automated lattice-surgery compiler for arbitrary multi-qubit Pauli measurements on a narrow-corridor 2D surface-code layout, with distance-preserving Y-measurement circuits and a wavefront partition that enables staged parallel decoding nearly matching monolithic decoding.
AI.motivation: Lattice surgery for arbitrary multi-qubit Pauli measurements is difficult to schedule and decode fault-tolerantly, especially for logical Y using twist defects; manual geometric rules are error-prone and monolithic decoding does not scale to real-time use.
AI.method: Compiler with systematic geometric rules for stabilizer placement and gate scheduling on a prescribed narrow-corridor layout; new measurement circuits and schedules with protruding Y-extension lobes; wavefront algorithm partitioning merged patches into space-time commit, buffer, and cleanup regions for staged decoding.
AI.result: Full effective code distance is preserved for all numerically tested distances. Simulations of three sequential multi-qubit Pauli measurements on ten logical qubits show staged decoding achieves total failure probabilities close to monolithic decoding over tested parameters.
AI.conclusion: Patchwork provides an automated fault-tolerant lattice-surgery framework and a route toward scalable real-time decoding.

title: Gyrators for superconducting circuit design
summary: Assuming only the solubility of Kirchhoff's laws, the conservation of energy, and the form of the constitutive relations, we present a flux-charge symmetric Hamiltonian formalism that always admits a symplectic reduction for nonsingular, well-posed circuits involving gyrators, inductors, and capacitors (LCG circuits) with arbitrary non-linearity. The formalism introduces a notion of circuit duality on non-linear non-reciprocal circuits and a family of point transformations that inserts, removes, and moves reciprocal elements across gyrators while preserving the Hamiltonian spectrum. With these transformations, we extend Tellegen's classic result that gyrators make reciprocal elements behave as their dual to non-linear reciprocal elements such as the Josephson junction and quantum phase slip. Furthermore, we present conditions under which non-reciprocal circuits can be transformed to dynamically equivalent reciprocal circuits.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a flux-charge symmetric Hamiltonian formalism for arbitrary nonlinear LCG circuits and uses symmetry transformations to extend Tellegen's gyrator-duality result to nonlinear elements and identify when non-reciprocal circuits are dynamically equivalent to reciprocal ones.
AI.motivation: Existing Hamiltonian circuit formalisms typically rely on reciprocity or linearity and lack a general symplectic-reduction treatment for nonlinear circuits containing gyrators; moreover, Tellegen's duality result for gyrators is established only for linear reciprocal elements, leaving the nonlinear case (e.g., Josephson junctions, quantum phase slips) open.
AI.method: A flux-charge symmetric Hamiltonian framework built solely on Kirchhoff's laws, energy conservation, and the constitutive relations, guaranteeing symplectic reduction for nonsingular, well-posed nonlinear LCG circuits. It introduces a circuit-duality notion for nonlinear non-reciprocal circuits and a family of point transformations that insert, remove, and move reciprocal elements across gyrators while preserving the Hamiltonian spectrum.
AI.result: The point transformations extend Tellegen's gyrator-duality result from linear reciprocal elements to nonlinear reciprocal elements such as the Josephson junction and quantum phase slip; explicit conditions are derived under which non-reciprocal circuits can be transformed into dynamically equivalent reciprocal circuits.
AI.conclusion: A unified, spectrum-preserving Hamiltonian framework for nonlinear LCG circuits is obtained, yielding a nonlinear circuit duality and a rigorous criterion for reciprocity restoration, applicable to superconducting quantum circuit design.

title: Connectivity Bounds for GHZ Graphs
summary: Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger (GHZ) states are multipartite entangled quantum states that play a central role in quantum information theory, with applications in quantum communication, cryptography, and distributed quantum computing. A major experimental goal is to create high-dimensional GHZ states using multiple entangled parties. Krenn, Gu and Zeilinger discovered a surprising bridge between these quantum-optical experiments and graph theory: certain photonic experiments can be represented by edge-coloured, edge-weighted graphs, and the dimension of the produced GHZ state equals the number of feasible monochromatic inherited vertex colourings. This led Krenn and Gu to conjecture that every GHZ graph with more than four vertices has dimension at most $2$. A counterexample would give a new high-dimensional multipartite GHZ construction, while a proof would clarify fundamental resource limitations in quantum optics. It is known that the conjecture holds for graphs of vertex connectivity at most $2$ [MFCS 2024], and that simple GHZ graphs with $n>4$ vertices have dimension less than $n/\sqrt{2}$ [Quantum 2024]. However, no general upper bound depending only on vertex connectivity was known. We prove that every simple connected GHZ graph $G$ with at least four vertices has dimension at most $2^{κ(G)-1}+\binom{κ(G)}{2}$, where $κ(G)$ is the vertex connectivity of $G$. We also prove new bounds in terms of edge connectivity and maximum degree.

AI.tldr: The paper proves that every simple connected GHZ graph with at least four vertices has GHZ dimension at most 2^{κ(G)-1} + C(κ(G),2), where κ(G) is the vertex connectivity, giving the first general upper bound depending only on connectivity; it also derives bounds via edge connectivity and maximum degree.
AI.motivation: Krenn and Gu conjectured that every GHZ graph with more than four vertices has dimension at most 2; a counterexample would yield a new high-dimensional multipartite GHZ construction, while a proof would expose fundamental resource limitations in quantum optics. Prior work established the conjecture only for vertex connectivity at most 2 and a dimension bound below n/√2, but no general connectivity-based upper bound was known.
AI.method: Combinatorial/graph-theoretic analysis of simple connected GHZ graphs, using the correspondence between photonic experiments and edge-coloured, edge-weighted graphs where the GHZ dimension equals the number of feasible monochromatic inherited vertex colourings. The analysis is parameterized by vertex connectivity κ(G), edge connectivity, and maximum degree.
AI.result: Every simple connected GHZ graph G with at least four vertices satisfies dim(G) ≤ 2^{κ(G)-1} + C(κ(G),2), and additional new upper bounds are obtained in terms of edge connectivity and maximum degree.
AI.conclusion: Vertex connectivity (and edge connectivity, maximum degree) governs the achievable GHZ dimension, providing a general structural constraint on high-dimensional multipartite GHZ constructions and clarifying resource limitations relevant to the Krenn–Gu conjecture.

title: Energetics of Fault-Tolerant Spin-Qubit Quantum Computation
comment: Keywords: Quantum Computation, Energetics, Spin-qubits, Semiconductors, Quantum Error Correction, Fault-Tolerant, Benchmarking
summary: Semiconductor spin qubits offer a promising route to compact and scalable quantum computers, combining long coherence times in isotopically purified silicon with compatibility with semiconductor manufacturing. Beyond computational speedup, their energy efficiency is an important consideration for future large-scale systems. We evaluate the power and energy requirements of a Loss-DiVincenzo spin-qubit quantum computer by analyzing the Quantum Fourier Transform (QFT) and benchmarking it against the classical Fast Fourier Transform (FFT). We develop a detailed energy budget, identifying cryogenic cooling as the dominant baseline contribution before quantum error correction (QEC). The comparison between the QFT and the classical FFT reveals that, for any quantum workload operating under a polynomially bounded sampling regime, the crossover in energy consumption occurs at smaller problem sizes than the crossover in execution time. Thus, quantum computing can become energetically competitive before achieving a speedup in execution time. We then incorporate surface-code QEC and analyze the energy costs of QEC cycles, gate synthesis, and decoding. At scale, instrumentation and decoding become dominant contributions, while cryogenic cooling imposes a constraint on scalability. We show that optimizing the control-signal demultiplexing ratio can reduce the overall energy cost by approximately two orders of magnitude. For a system with about one million physical qubits, we estimate a power consumption of approximately 100 kW, at least one order of magnitude below that of today's highest-performance classical computing systems.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates the power and energy requirements of a Loss–DiVincenzo silicon spin-qubit quantum computer running the QFT, benchmarks it against the classical FFT, and includes surface-code QEC. Energy crossover with FFT occurs at smaller problem sizes than the time crossover, and optimized control-signal demultiplexing cuts energy cost ~100x; a ~1M-qubit system is estimated at ~100 kW.
AI.motivation: Semiconductor spin qubits are attractive for scalable quantum computing, but beyond speedup their energy efficiency is a key open consideration for future large-scale systems; prior work has not systematically quantified power/energy budgets including cryogenics and QEC.
AI.method: Builds a detailed energy budget for a Loss–DiVincenzo spin-qubit machine executing the QFT, benchmarked against the classical FFT, first in the pre-QEC regime and then with surface-code QEC (analyzing QEC cycle energy, gate synthesis, and decoding costs). Control-signal demultiplexing ratio is optimized.
AI.result: Cryogenic cooling dominates the baseline pre-QEC budget; for polynomially bounded sampling, the energy crossover versus FFT occurs at smaller problem sizes than the execution-time crossover. With QEC at scale, instrumentation and decoding dominate, cryogenics constrain scalability, and optimized demultiplexing reduces total energy by ~2 orders of magnitude; a ~1M physical-qubit system is estimated at ~100 kW, ≥10x below top classical systems.
AI.conclusion: Quantum computing can become energetically competitive with classical FFT before achieving an execution-time speedup, and spin-qubit systems with surface-code QEC may offer favorable power scaling, contingent on cryogenic and demultiplexing engineering.

title: Efficient quantum simulation of unitary gates based on atomic ensembles
summary: We develop a technique to perform efficient unitary time evolution of a general spin Hamiltonian based on the system with identical qubits, as naturally realized by permutation symmetric atomic ensembles. We employ Cartan decomposition method to the associated Hamiltonian Lie algebra and construct the symmetry adapted generators to implement unitary operator of the ensemble Hamiltonian. This enables the compact circuit representations of the system dynamics in terms of experimentally accessible collective spin operations and exploits the Dicke basis structure of the ensembles as an effective qudit representation. We benchmark Cartan based evolution against both exact time evolution and the Suzuki Trotter product formula. Our results show that the Cartan protocol accurately reproduces the operator dynamics, spin expectation values, and fluctuation observables with zero error that are substantially smaller than those obtained through Trotterization while maintaining an optimized circuit structure. In addition, scaling analysis with the ensemble size demonstrates that the Cartan error remains independent of the atom number while the corresponding Trotter error increases with the system size, highlighting the improved efficiency of the Cartan approach for a larger system size.

AI.tldr: A Cartan-decomposition-based scheme for efficient unitary time evolution of permutation-symmetric spin ensembles, giving compact circuits with system-size-independent error far outperforming Suzuki-Trotter.
AI.motivation: Simulating unitary time evolution of general spin Hamiltonians on identical-qubit (permutation-symmetric) ensembles is costly with standard product-formula approaches, since Trotter errors grow with system size. A more efficient, symmetry-exploiting method is needed.
AI.method: Apply Cartan decomposition to the Hamiltonian Lie algebra and build symmetry-adapted generators to construct the ensemble unitary operator. This yields compact circuits using experimentally accessible collective spin operations and exploits the Dicke basis as an effective qudit representation.
AI.result: Benchmarked against exact evolution and Suzuki-Trotter, the Cartan protocol reproduces operator dynamics, spin expectation values, and fluctuation observables with essentially zero error, far below Trotterization, while keeping an optimized circuit. Scaling analysis shows Cartan error is independent of atom number, whereas Trotter error grows with system size.
AI.conclusion: Cartan decomposition provides an accurate, compact, and size-scalable approach for simulating permutation-symmetric spin ensemble dynamics, becoming increasingly advantageous over Trotterization for larger ensembles.

title: Programmable all-to-all entangling gates for cavity-coupled atoms
summary: Fault tolerant quantum computers greatly benefit from having both high fidelity entangling gates and a non-local qubit connectivity. However, most entangling gates for neutral atoms are local, requiring separated atoms to be moved using optical tweezers to yield entanglement between them. Here, we design a high fidelity Mølmer Sørensen-like entangling gate between neutral atoms coupled to a photonic cavity, enabling a programmable all-to-all connectivity through the shared cavity coupling. The gate is both robust to changes in cavity photon number, and enables selective entanglement between any subset of separated atoms through local laser addressing. This eliminates the need to physically move atoms to perform the gate, and therefore motional errors and erasure are suppressed. Using experimentally realistic parameters we demonstrate gate fidelities exceeding $F > 0.99$, with higher fidelities achievable through optimal control of the pump amplitudes.

AI.tldr: A cavity-mediated Mølmer–Sørensen-like entangling gate for neutral atoms that provides programmable all-to-all connectivity without physically moving atoms, achieving fidelities above 0.99.
AI.motivation: Fault-tolerant quantum computing needs both high-fidelity entangling gates and non-local qubit connectivity, but most neutral-atom entangling gates are local and require optical-tweezer transport of separated atoms, which introduces motional errors and erasure.
AI.method: The authors design a Mølmer–Sørensen-type entangling gate between neutral atoms coupled to a shared photonic cavity, using local laser addressing for selective entanglement and pump-amplitude optimal control. The gate is designed to be robust to cavity photon-number fluctuations.
AI.result: With experimentally realistic parameters, gate fidelities exceeding F > 0.99 are demonstrated, with even higher fidelities achievable through optimal control of pump amplitudes.
AI.conclusion: Cavity-mediated MS-like gates enable programmable all-to-all connectivity between stationary neutral atoms, eliminating transport-induced motional errors and erasure while maintaining high fidelity suitable for fault-tolerant architectures.

title: Constrained dissipation and the lifetime of quantum many-body scars
comment: 6 pages, 4 figures; plus 6 pages of Supplemental Material (3 figures)
summary: We investigate the fate of quantum many-body scars in the PXP model subject to Markovian dissipation. We show that when local jump operators respect the same symmetries of the Hamiltonian the full Liouvillian spectrum displays a tower of states with properties analogous to standard quantum scars: large overlaps with Néel states and equally spaced gaps in the imaginary part of the eigenvalues, set by a single frequency. Whether the long-time dynamics is dominated by scars is determined by the real parts of the eigenvalues, which are set by the ratio between the two relaxation rates $γ_{\pm}$ describing spin flips down-to-up or up-to-down respectively. For asymmetric dissipation ($γ_+ > γ_-$) the scarred eigenvalues have the smallest real parts: the resulting enhanced fidelity oscillations are further stabilized by staggered jump operators. In contrast, replacing the full projection operator in the dissipators with a partial one breaks the symmetries of the problem and is seen to destroy dissipative scars altogether.

AI.tldr: The authors study quantum many-body scars in the PXP model under Markovian dissipation and show that symmetry-respecting jump operators preserve a scarred tower in the Liouvillian spectrum, whose long-time relevance is controlled by the asymmetry of relaxation rates.
AI.motivation: Quantum scars were established in isolated (unitary) PXP dynamics, but realistic systems are open and subject to dissipation. Whether scar-induced coherent oscillations survive Markovian dissipation, and what determines their dominance at long times, was unclear.
AI.method: Lindblad master equation for the PXP model with local jump operators; Liouvillian spectral analysis. The jump operators are chosen to respect the symmetries of the Hamiltonian. The resulting Liouvillian eigenmodes are characterized by their overlaps with Néel states and by the structure (imaginary parts, i.e. equally spaced gaps set by a single frequency) of the scarred tower. Two relaxation rates γ+ and γ− for spin flips down-to-up and up-to-down control the real parts of the eigenvalues. The role of staggered jump operators and of replacing the full projection operator by a partial one is examined.
AI.result: When jump operators respect the Hamiltonian symmetries, the full Liouvillian spectrum contains a scarred tower with large overlaps with Néel states and equally spaced imaginary-part gaps fixed by one frequency. Long-time dynamics is governed by the real parts, set by the ratio γ+/γ−. For asymmetric dissipation (γ+ > γ−), scarred eigenvalues have the smallest real parts, giving enhanced, long-lived fidelity oscillations, which are further stabilized by staggered jump operators. Using a partial projection operator in the dissipators breaks the symmetries and destroys the dissipative scars.
AI.conclusion: Dissipative quantum many-body scars are symmetry-protected: they persist in the Liouvillian spectrum provided the jump operators inherit the Hamiltonian's symmetries, and their dominance at long times is controlled by the asymmetry of the relaxation rates, with staggered dissipation enhancing stability. Breaking symmetry via partial projections eliminates them.

title: SynDebug: A Framework to Debug Logic Bugs in Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computing Programs
comment: SynDebug will appear at SIGOPS ATC 2026
summary: Fault-tolerant quantum computing (FTQC) introduces substantial systems-level complexity through quantum error correction (QEC), making debugging FTQC programs challenging. Existing quantum debugging approaches primarily target logical-level circuits and do not naturally support debugging within realistic FTQC execution flows. We present SynDebug, the first systems-level debugging framework for FTQC programs. SynDebug introduces lightweight assertion-based debugging primitives that operate directly within encoded FTQC infrastructures while avoiding additional logical surface area and minimizing temporal overhead. We evaluate SynDebug across multiple QEC code families, code distances, and encoded workloads, including state preparation, entanglement validation, and Shor-style programs. Our results demonstrate that SynDebug enables practical FTQC debugging with an average 1.8% additional circuit depth overhead (0% in most cases) and no measurable increase in the logical error rate, showing that systems-level debugging for large-scale FTQC applications is both feasible and practical.

AI.tldr: SynDebug is the first systems-level assertion-based debugging framework for fault-tolerant quantum computing programs, achieving low overhead (avg 1.8% extra depth) without increasing logical error rates.
AI.motivation: FTQC introduces systems-level complexity via QEC, making FTQC programs hard to debug. Existing quantum debuggers target logical-level circuits and don't fit realistic FTQC execution flows, creating a gap for systems-level debugging support.
AI.method: Lightweight assertion-based debugging primitives that operate directly within encoded FTQC infrastructures, avoiding additional logical surface area and minimizing temporal overhead. Evaluated across multiple QEC code families, code distances, and encoded workloads (state preparation, entanglement validation, Shor-style programs).
AI.result: Average 1.8% additional circuit depth overhead (0% in most cases) and no measurable increase in the logical error rate.
AI.conclusion: Systems-level debugging for large-scale FTQC applications is both feasible and practical, demonstrating SynDebug enables practical FTQC debugging.

title: Classical Capacity of Single-Mode Bosonic Gaussian Channels
comment: 24 pages, 2 figures. See also related results for entanglement in https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01909v3
summary: The classical capacity of a noisy optical channel is the maximum rate at which information can be transmitted reliably, given a constraint on the mean input energy. For the ubiquitous bosonic Gaussian channels, which include standard models of loss and noise in fibre and free-space optical links, determining this rate requires addressing whether entanglement between channel uses or non-Gaussian signals can outperform Gaussian encodings. More precisely, the question is whether the energy-constrained Holevo information is additive across arbitrarily many channel uses and coincides with its Gaussian counterpart. We answer these fundamental questions in the affirmative for every single-mode bosonic Gaussian channel at every input energy. Namely, we prove that independently prepared Gaussian states with Gaussian-distributed random displacements achieve the capacity, including in the low-energy regime where squeezing the signals competes with encoding information in their displacement. Our proof connects an entanglement inequality to a sharp, additive lower bound on output entropy. We then characterise communication above capacity: under a strict total photon-number cutoff, the probability of correct decoding decreases exponentially with the number of channel uses, and we derive explicit bounds on the decay exponent. When only the mean photon number is constrained, a simple energy-rescaling formula determines exactly the entire asymptotic rate--error trade-off: the capacity at mean photon number $N$ and allowed average decoding error $ε$ equals the vanishing-error capacity at mean photon number $N/(1-ε)$. Together, these results identify the ultimate limits of classical communication for some of the most fundamental models of optical communication.

AI.tldr: This paper proves that Gaussian encodings with Gaussian-distributed random displacements achieve the classical capacity of every single-mode bosonic Gaussian channel at every input energy, that the energy-constrained Holevo information is additive and equals its Gaussian counterpart, and it characterizes the rate-error trade-off above capacity.
AI.motivation: For bosonic Gaussian channels (models of loss and noise in fibre and free-space optical links), the classical capacity requires resolving whether entanglement across channel uses or non-Gaussian signals can outperform Gaussian encodings—i.e., whether the energy-constrained Holevo information is additive over arbitrarily many uses and equals its Gaussian value.
AI.method: The authors prove additivity by connecting an entanglement inequality to a sharp, additive lower bound on the output entropy. The optimal encoding uses independently prepared Gaussian states with Gaussian-distributed random displacements, covering the low-energy regime where squeezing competes with displacement encoding. Above-capacity behaviour is analyzed under a strict total photon-number cutoff and under a mean photon-number constraint.
AI.result: Additivity and Gaussian optimality are established affirmatively for every single-mode bosonic Gaussian channel at every input energy. Under a strict total photon-number cutoff, the decoding success probability decays exponentially with the number of channel uses, with explicit bounds on the decay exponent. Under a mean photon-number constraint, the capacity at mean photon number N and average error ε equals the vanishing-error capacity at mean photon number N/(1−ε).
AI.conclusion: Gaussian encodings are optimal for classical communication over single-mode bosonic Gaussian channels, and a simple energy-rescaling formula exactly determines the full asymptotic rate-error trade-off, identifying the ultimate limits of classical optical communication.

title: Magna: simulating magic state factories as cheaply as Clifford circuits
summary: Classical simulation of magic state factories, including distillation, cultivation, and code switching, is challenging because of their substantial non-Clifford content. We introduce $\texttt{magna}$ (magic-state-factory assessment via global network algebra), a classical simulator that simulates such protocols as cheaply as Clifford circuits. $\texttt{magna}$ expresses the figures of merit of a protocol, namely the acceptance rate and the fidelity of the accepted states, as tensor networks, which it reduces globally by exploiting a structural correspondence with transversal gates on quantum codes. $\texttt{magna}$ further supports feedforward conditioned on arbitrary functions of mid-circuit measurement outcomes, including decoder outputs. We simulate Bravyi--Haah distillation with up to 100 output magic states at a cost that does not grow exponentially in the number of outputs, and achieve state-of-the-art sampling times for distance-5 magic state cultivation on both color codes and RP$^2$ surface codes. Finally, we validate nonlinear feedforward on a logical-level distillation protocol with 15 rounds of decoder-dependent feedforward. $\texttt{magna}$ aims to contribute to the key infrastructure for the large-scale evaluation and optimization of magic state factories.

AI.tldr: $\texttt{magna}$ is a classical simulator that evaluates magic state factories—distillation, cultivation, and code switching—as cheaply as Clifford circuits by expressing figures of merit as tensor networks reduced via a structural correspondence with transversal gates on quantum codes.
AI.motivation: Magic state factories contain substantial non-Clifford content, which makes classical simulation of their protocols (distillation, cultivation, code switching) challenging. Efficient evaluation is needed for large-scale assessment and optimization of these factories.
AI.method: $\texttt{magna}$ (magic-state-factory assessment via global network algebra) expresses a protocol's figures of merit—acceptance rate and fidelity of accepted states—as tensor networks, then reduces them globally by exploiting a structural correspondence with transversal gates on quantum codes. It also supports feedforward conditioned on arbitrary functions of mid-circuit measurement outcomes, including decoder outputs. Its cost scales like Clifford-circuit simulation.
AI.result: The simulator handles Bravyi–Haah distillation with up to 100 output magic states at a cost that does not grow exponentially in the number of outputs, achieves state-of-the-art sampling times for distance-5 magic state cultivation on both color codes and RP$^2$ surface codes, and validates nonlinear feedforward on a logical-level distillation protocol with 15 rounds of decoder-dependent feedforward.
AI.conclusion: $\texttt{magna}$ provides efficient classical simulation of non-Clifford magic state factories and aims to serve as key infrastructure for large-scale evaluation and optimization of magic state factories.

title: Magic in quantum trajectory unravelings of noisy random quantum circuits
summary: The quantum-trajectory description of a noisy quantum circuit is not unique: every Kraus representation of the noise channel defines a different unraveling, i.e., a different ensemble of pure states that averages to the same density matrix. While all unravelings share the same expectation values of observables, they generally differ in the amount of quantum resources carried by the individual trajectories. Here we study non-stabilizerness, or magic, quantified by the stabilizer Rényi entropy, in quantum-trajectory unravelings of Haar-random and $T$-doped random Clifford brickwork circuits subject to local dephasing noise of strength $p$. The canonical unraveling in terms of Pauli jumps is Clifford and leaves magic untouched, so that trajectories retain the Haar-random value of non-stabilizerness. Exploring the full two-parameter family of minimal unravelings, we find that the trajectory-averaged magic can be substantially reduced by a state-independent choice of Kraus operators, and that the optimal choice is not in general the projective-measurement unraveling, but a two-outcome generalized measurement in which the Kraus operators correspond to a weak measurement of the noisy qubit. The optimal unraveling reduces the extensive magic density of the trajectories by a $p$-dependent factor without altering its linear scaling with system size. At the same time, it produces a very broad distribution of magic over trajectories, with a sizable fraction of trajectories retaining Haar-random magic. Since the cost of stabilizer-based classical simulation grows exponentially with the magic of the state, these high-magic trajectories, rather than the average, control the simulation cost. Our results delineate the potential and the limitations of unraveling optimization as a route to the classical simulation of noisy quantum dynamics with stabilizer methods.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how the choice of Kraus (unraveling) representation of local dephasing noise affects the non-stabilizerness (magic) of quantum trajectories, finding that a state-independent two-outcome weak-measurement unraveling minimizes average magic density by a p-dependent factor but leaves linear scaling and a broad distribution with near-Haar-random high-magic trajectories that dominate stabilizer-based simulation cost.
AI.motivation: Quantum trajectories are not unique: each Kraus representation of a noise channel gives a different pure-state ensemble with identical observables but different resource content. Since stabilizer-based classical simulation cost scales exponentially with magic, it is important to know whether choosing an optimal unraveling can suppress trajectory magic and thus enable efficient simulation of noisy quantum dynamics.
AI.method: The authors quantify magic via the stabilizer Rényi entropy for Haar-random and T-doped random Clifford brickwork circuits under local dephasing of strength p. They compare the canonical Pauli-jump unraveling (Clifford, magic-preserving) with the full two-parameter family of minimal unravelings, searching for state-independent Kraus operators that minimize trajectory-averaged magic, and analyze the resulting magic distribution across trajectories.
AI.result: The canonical Pauli unraveling leaves magic at the Haar-random value. The trajectory-averaged magic can be substantially reduced by a state-independent Kraus choice, and the optimum is generally not the projective-measurement unraveling but a two-outcome generalized (weak) measurement of the noisy qubit. The optimal unraveling reduces the extensive magic density by a p-dependent factor without changing its linear system-size scaling, while producing a broad magic distribution in which a sizable fraction of trajectories retain Haar-random magic.
AI.conclusion: Because stabilizer simulation cost grows exponentially with state magic, the high-magic tail—not the average—governs simulation cost, so unraveling optimization offers only limited advantage: it delineates the potential and limitations of this route for classically simulating noisy quantum dynamics with stabilizer methods.

title: Stability of Quantum LDPC States under Local Pauli Noise
summary: Quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) codes have a canonical mixed state---the normalized projector onto the code space---that lies at the intersection of quantum error correction and quantum many-body physics, yet the stability of its information-theoretic structure under local noise remains poorly understood. Recent progress on mixed-state phases of matter has identified the spatial decay of conditional mutual information (CMI) $I(A:C|B)$ as a key diagnostic of such stability, analogous to the role of the spectral gap for quantum ground states. We prove that, for the normalized code-projector state of a $\mathbb{Z}_d$ qLDPC stabilizer code under local Pauli noise, the CMI across a buffer $B$ separating $A$ from $C$ decays exponentially with the width of $B$ in two complementary noise regimes independent of system size. At weak noise, this holds for full-system tripartitions, where correlations between the two sides require an error cluster to cross the buffer, an exponentially unlikely event. At strong noise, exponential decay holds whenever the buffer supports no logical operator, since correlations can persist only along rare chains of buffer qudits that remain informative. Under an additional space-uniformity assumption, we establish the robustness of Levin--Wen topological entropy. On finite-dimensional lattices of size $n$, the weak-noise bound further implies a constant-layer quasi-local Petz recovery channel of range $O(\poly(\log n)/\varepsilon)$ that recovers the noiseless state within trace-distance error $\varepsilon$. Both CMI bounds apply to general qLDPC interaction graphs, including geometries where such constant-depth quasi-local recovery need not exist. Thus, the exponential decay of the noise-induced CMI provides a general criterion for mixed-state phase stability.

AI.tldr: The paper proves that the conditional mutual information (CMI) across a buffer separating two regions decays exponentially with the buffer's width for the normalized code-projector state of a Z_d qLDPC stabilizer code under local Pauli noise, in two noise regimes (weak and strong), independent of system size, establishing CMI decay as a general criterion for mixed-state phase stability and implying robustness of Levin–Wen topological entropy plus a constant-layer quasi-local Petz recovery channel.
AI.motivation: The normalized projector onto the code space of a qLDPC code is a canonical mixed state at the intersection of quantum error correction and many-body physics, but the stability of its information-theoretic structure under local noise is poorly understood. The spatial decay of CMI I(A:C|B) has been proposed as a key diagnostic of mixed-state phase stability (analogous to the spectral gap for ground states), so a rigorous understanding of CMI behavior under local noise is needed.
AI.method: Proves exponential decay of CMI I(A:C|B) across a buffer B separating A and C, with decay exponential in the buffer width and independent of system size, for the code-projector state under local Pauli noise, treating two complementary regimes: weak noise (full-system tripartitions, where cross-buffer correlations require an exponentially unlikely error cluster to cross B) and strong noise (buffers supporting no logical operator, where correlations persist only along rare informative chains of buffer qudits). Also derives, under a space-uniformity assumption, robustness of Levin–Wen topological entropy, and on finite-dimensional lattices a constant-layer quasi-local Petz recovery channel.
AI.result: CMI decays exponentially with buffer width in both weak- and strong-noise regimes, independent of system size. Under an added space-uniformity assumption, Levin–Wen topological entropy is robust. On finite-dimensional lattices of size n, the weak-noise bound yields a constant-layer quasi-local Petz recovery channel of range O(poly(log n)/ε) that recovers the noiseless state within trace-distance error ε. The CMI bounds hold for general qLDPC interaction graphs, including geometries where constant-depth quasi-local recovery need not exist.
AI.conclusion: Exponential decay of the noise-induced CMI provides a general criterion for mixed-state phase stability, applying broadly to general qLDPC interaction graphs (beyond geometries admitting constant-depth quasi-local recovery), and yields robustness of topological entropy and quasi-local recoverability as consequences.

title: Discovering state-of-the-art quantum circuits with large language models
summary: Significant efforts are currently being directed toward the implementation of large-scale quantum information processors, but realizing useful quantum advantage also requires the development of efficient quantum algorithms. While for many practical problems the dominant resource costs are associated with a small set of computational primitives, optimizing them in the quantum setting presents unique challenges, including a reversibility constraint absent from ordinary classical computation. Here we introduce an evolutionary framework in which large language models (LLMs) propose circuit designs and an independent evaluator verifies and scores them. We apply this framework to tasks spanning numerical computation, chemistry, optimization, quantum simulation, and number theory. In seven of the eight tasks, the discovered circuits significantly reduce both Toffoli and qubit counts relative to the state of the art. In the eighth, the search discovers a new reversible architecture for prime-field modular inversion. By handling reversibility differently, the architecture makes divsteps -- a classical algorithm previously impractical for reversible integer arithmetic -- viable and substantially improves the Toffoli-qubit trade-off for modular inversion. These results open the door for evaluator-guided LLM co-design of new algorithmic structures for quantum computation.

AI.tldr: An evolutionary framework where LLMs propose quantum circuit designs and an independent evaluator verifies and scores them finds circuits that reduce Toffoli and qubit counts across numerical computation, chemistry, optimization, quantum simulation, and number theory tasks.
AI.motivation: Realizing quantum advantage requires efficient quantum algorithms, and the dominant resource costs (Toffoli and qubit counts) concentrate in a small set of computational primitives. Optimizing these primitives is uniquely challenging in the quantum setting due to the reversibility constraint absent in ordinary classical computation.
AI.method: The authors introduce an evolutionary framework in which large language models propose circuit designs and an independent evaluator verifies and scores them, iterating to guide circuit discovery. They apply it to eight tasks spanning numerical computation, chemistry, optimization, quantum simulation, and number theory.
AI.result: In seven of eight tasks, discovered circuits significantly reduce both Toffoli and qubit counts relative to the state of the art. In the eighth, the search discovers a new reversible architecture for prime-field modular inversion that makes divsteps (a classical algorithm previously impractical for reversible integer arithmetic) viable and substantially improves the Toffoli-qubit trade-off.
AI.conclusion: Evaluator-guided LLM co-design opens the door to discovering new algorithmic structures for quantum computation, with the framework yielding state-of-the-art circuit improvements and a novel reversible architecture for modular inversion.
